An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Additionally, the total branching fraction of this decay was determined to be in the range $(3.8±0.5±0.3)×10^{-5}$, and a search for resonance contributions yielded none above 1.5 standard deviation for any potential particle. The results were consistent with Standard Model predictions and did not reveal any significant evidence for new physics. A more precise measurement of $B^0_s\rightarrow μ^+μ^-$ decays using around 35 picobarns of 2010 LHCb data found a branching fraction of $(0.36±0.09±0.05)×10^{-6}$, and with various assumptions on form factor behaviour, a total decay rate of $(4.8±1.2±0.6±0.3)×10^{-6}$ ps$^{-1}$. These results are in line with expectations from the Standard Model and contribute meaningfully to the existing body of knowledge on this topic. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We anticipate that future observations, incorporating additional data from the Southern Giant Air Shower Observatory, will enable more precise investigations due to its significantly larger detection area and integrated exposure at the highest energy levels. We also outline strategies for optimizing the detection of such patterns in future experiments. Finally, we discuss the relevance of our findings to the extragalactic origin of the highest-energy cosmic rays, reaffirming that an isotropic distribution cannot adequately account for the observed patterns and anisotropy indices. We also propose specific methods for distinguishing between cosmic source distributions within the stratosphere and the cosmic ray anisotropy patterns they generate. We conclude that a uniform distribution of sources across the sky cannot be consistent with the observed patterns of extremely energetic cosmic ray anisotropy. We anticipate that future studies will provide greater clarity on the orientation and spatial density of these sources. We also outline specific approaches for identifying the cosmic magnetic field lines linking the sources to the detectors, and presenting the cosmic ray patterns as a map of the electromagnetic field across the sky. Lastly, we suggest that the most energetic cosmic ray detectors should be optimized for detecting the global pattern of cosmic rays rather than identifying single-air-shower events. We further propose that a comprehensive theoretical framework for extremely energetic cosmic rays should incorporate the distribution of these sources and the associated cosmic ray patterns, treating the sky as a continuous, integrated system. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further optimize the federated training process, we explored the impact of differing dataset sizes at each location on the performance of models and identified key sources of bias within the federation. Finally, we highlight potential issues that may limit the adoption of federated learning in practice, while also suggesting possible strategies to address these challenges. The techniques and insights shared in this work can serve as a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the feasibility and effectiveness of federated learning in image analysis applications. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. The optimized WDFFE-MLE system was found to offer up to 2.9dB improvement in signal quality and eliminate BER floors in certain scenarios. The development of this optimized system may provide a viable solution for addressing burst-error propagation issues in fiber-optic communications systems. The optimized WDFFE-MLE system was evaluated at data rates of 10, 24, 36 and 48Gbit/s and demonstrated effective compensation for a 18.8km underwater cable without dispersion compensation, itself a notable achievement. The successful application of this technique may open up new possibilities for the reliable transmission of high-speed data signals through submarine cables. The reliable transmission of these signals is critical for the healthy operation of high-speed underwater networks in remote regions connected to the global internet. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our approach is a versatile framework that can be integrated into any TCN variant and extends to other convolutional networks. We demonstrate the benefits of this method in two Inference Scenarios: sequential prediction and single-instance prediction. In the former, we outperform state-of-the-art models for large-scale time-series classification. In the latter, we showcase robust performance across various single-instance time-series tasks. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdwu/Pruning-Dilated-TCN. The paper is openly published on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07295. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. Moreover, this reversal method is demonstrated to be computationally efficient and straightforward to execute in practice. Additionally, we explore potential applications including the enhancement of ALBA's functionality to handle additional operators and the development of tactics within the theorem proving environment TTT2. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a comprehensive framework for interacting with the algebraic content of logics within the TTT2 environment. Full-scale protocols for computing the second-order correspondents or deciding canonicity along specific axes appear to be more complex issues. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Building on this work, potential applications and future directions for further exploration have been identified. These directions are connected to the broader theme of handling inconsistencies in data tables and raise crucial considerations concerning data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging within the context of bidirectional reasoning. Lastly, we outline an actionable plan to tackle these directions through the development of advanced data repair mechanisms that can handle not only inconsistencies but also temporal relationships in data tables. As a starting point, we introduce a query validation problem and provide an innovative solution linked to Four-valued logic, and related to but distinct from data repair scenarios. Nevertheless, numerous pressing problems and research questions remain unanswered, such as how to handle concurrent repairs, multi-relational repairs, and distributed repair scenarios, to name a few. Consequently, this work is seen as an initial step towards a more comprehensive theory for handling inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships, with significant implications for data quality assessments, query validation, data merging, and related data management tasks. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our research findings indicate that the TV-PARX approach forecasts count-based time series data more accurately than alternative models, including the traditional PARX model, subject to distributional assumptions. Forecasts produced by using the TV-PARX model's recursive algorithm are also compared to those obtained from generalized method state specifications, showing competitive results. All necessary software code and data sets are available for replication and further research purposes.

replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. The lack of straggling stars at the low metal content end and the presence of multiple blue horizontal branch members within the cluster support the theoretical hypothesis that blue horizontal branch members within globular clusters are primarily the result of esoteric processes. The finding of a nitrogen spread and small s-process enriched population within Tononzintla 2 highlights the diversity that exists among rich-metallic galactic globular clusters and could be attributed to unique birth environment conditions. The results of this analysis will be contributing to ongoing research on the chemistry and dynamics of the galaxy.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Building on this insight, I plan to investigate various search strategies and their efficacy in comparing them to traditional breadth-first search, as well as to develop a visualization tool to help stakeholders navigate the archive by means of dependency graphs. Additionally, I aim to examine the statistical properties of proof development sizes and their relationships with paper lengths, as well as to identify potential barriers to entry in the field of theorem proving, all of which will be underpinned by a theoretical framework informed by information theory and the economics of knowledge reuse. Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These results can be used to set a lower bound on the temperature at which one-side universality begins to dominate in QCD, essentially above $T \approx 0.65 T_c$ for the three-dimensional Ising universality class. Additionally, we have investigated the Yang-Lee edge singularity in the pure QCD universality class beyond classic scenarios, specifically for the Z(2) axion model where we found the relevant perturbation to drive one-side universality dominance, and set a lower bound on the mass scale at which this dominance starts to dominate in this scenario. If the relevant parameter is near its expected value of $m_\Lambda \approx 0.65 T_c^3$, we suggest that one-side universality in QCD could be investigated in future lattice simulations. If the relevant parameter is far from this value, a more precise location of the Yang-Lee edge singularity might be required to conclusively determine one-side universality dominance. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our technique may be useful in investigating the ease with which various sampling algorithms solve certain problems. The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This theoretical validation relies heavily on key concepts, including the formal orbital linearization theorem for formally integrable vector fields, the application of the blowing-up technique, and the application of the Sternberg-Chen theorem regarding formally equivalent smooth hyperbolic vector fields. Moreover, this research establishes a significant new application for the blowing-up technique in the context of smooth local differential dynamics. Additionally, this research contributes a new approach to the study of the orbital linearization problem for smooth vector fields. Lastly, this research implies the existence of formally and smoothly orbitally equivalent hyperbolic vector fields with nonresonant eigenvalues near a nondegenerate singular point. This last implication is particularly noteworthy as it resolves a long-standing openness question regarding the orbital equivalence of hyperbolic vector fields with nonresonant eigenvalues near a nondegenerate singular point. Lastly, this research validates the hypothesis of the formal orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This validation extends the applicability of this hypothesis to include vector fields with nondegenerate singular points having nonresonant eigenvalues and those that are conjugate to a linear rotation near a degenerate singular point. Furthermore, this research also validates the hypothesis of the formal orbital linearization theorem for smoothly formally equivalent hyperbolic vector fields, whether they have a nondegenerate singular point or are conjugate to a linear rotation near a degenerate singular point. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. To
demonstrate its effectiveness, we train and test the eCPNN framework on a diverse set
of 30 two-dimensional atoms ranging from hydrogen to carbon dioxide and spanning
excited states and configurations where a single electron is promoted to a higher
energy shell. Our results show that the eCPNN potential functions obtain an average
accuracy of 0.35 electrons/bohr^2 in density comparisons and yield atomic energy
predictions that closely match the original values with an average difference of 0.04
eV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the eCPNN model can be an efficient and
versatile tool for various atomic physics applications by demonstrating its
utility in calculating static and dynamic form factors, hyperfines, and electron
spatial correlations. Additionally, we explore the potential of this deep learning
approach to handle three-dimensional atomic systems and outline future development
directions for the eCPNN framework. All data used in this study and implemented
in the eCPNN package are available online at https://github.com/pankaj312/ecomms.

We have serendipitously identified a massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. The Giant Arc represents one of the largest and most intriguing examples of a massive cosmic structure that could challenge the cosmological principle underpinning our current understanding of the universe. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age. The discovery of the Giant Arc highlights the value of using absorption lines to identify large-scale structures and suggests that a systematic survey of this type has the potential to uncover more massive cosmic features hidden behind bright background sources. It also sets the stage for follow-up observations of the Giant Arc, which could provide critical insights through spectroscopic studies of the structure itself. It is essential that any such investigations account for the effects of the Giant Arc on the observed spectra, taking care to correct for any contamination from the massive cosmic structure. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Before collecting field data, we performed calibration experiments to establish a reliable method for determining the optical density of aerosols and systematically assessing the data's validity. The result of these efforts was a precision of approximately 0.01 achieved in the vertical aerosol optical density measurement. Ultimately, this technique was applied to study the coexistence of different aerosol types and the movement of aerosol plumes at the Southern Atlantic Ocean. The technique's sensitivity was also enhanced to detect sources with low optical density, such as plumes rising over the surrounding aerosol field, through the use of optimized spectral filters. The technique has the potential to contribute to ground-based aerosol research and provide valuable data for satellite sensor calibration. The method has been made publicly available to facilitate the analysis of similar data collections at the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Cherenkov Telescope Array. The code and data can be accessed through the CALEO collaboration repository at https://github.com/alexx-y/CALEO-Aerosols. The study has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation, Volume 13, Number 1, 2024. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code has been made publicly available.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average bias in solvent simulations. As a result, this research may facilitate more efficient molecular dynamics simulations, especially in complex systems. Lastly, the investigation introduced an intuitive measure for evaluating numerical integration algorithms in molecular dynamics simulations, namely the configurational average bias factor, which can serve as a straightforward performance indicator for comparing different methods. This research is part of an ongoing project aiming to develop an open-source numerical integration toolkit that is available under the MIT license and can be obtained from an open repository. Overall, the study presents an evaluation of high-order methods for molecular dynamics simulations, introducing a new benchmark that can be employed to assess the precision of numerical integrators in molecular dynamics simulations, and provides an open-source implementation that can be used for molecular dynamics simulations in vacuum and in solution, using both alanine dipeptide and small biomolecules as models. This open-source implementation is compatible with well-established molecular mechanics force fields, such as AMBER. Lastly, the research is part of an ongoing project that aims to develop an open-source toolkit for developing numerical integration methods, incorporating user feedback and enabling seamless comparison of algorithm performance. This comparison can be conducted over cloud services, facilitating collaborative research. Ultimately, this research is oriented towards developing a robust, high-performance, and highly configurable molecular dynamics software framework that can be used for both small and large biomolecular systems. Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts. In order to facilitate such comparison, we've developed a method for removing artificial oscillations present in simulations involving dark matter, by effectively removing the dark matter's initial distortions that arise prior to the starting point of the simulation. As such, we believe this methodology will be an invaluable tool in future studies aimed at uncovering the signature of dark matter in gravitational waves. In order to validate our method, we've conducted a range of tests, including: (one) a perfect test, where we removed artificial oscillations in a simulation conducted in a vacuum, despite it being classified as an environment-based simulation; (two) an imperfect test, where we compared our method against alternative approaches aimed at eliminating artificial oscillations in a broader range of scenarios; (three) a gravitational wave waveform comparison, where we compared our method against alternative approaches aimed at eliminating artificial oscillations in a broader range of scenarios, including KN solutions, where we found that only our method successfully eliminated artificial oscillations in all instances. Ultimately, we believe that our method represents a significant step forward in preparing the binary black hole merger simulations for further analysis, and is poised to play a key role in any future search for dark matter in gravitational waves. We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. Additionally, we explore how friction's absence complicates the spectrum's assembly, and provide evidence that more rigid connections are necessary to guarantee uniform stability. Finally, we apply our general approach to a specific setup, and contrast our findings with existing related research.

Researchers utilized acoustic lenses composed of PMMA to increase the detection area of sensitive devices and improve resolution but discovered these lenses introduced image distortion. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology. Though the degree of distortion remained moderate and likely wouldn't impede imaging functionality in real-world applications, it highlights the need for correction algorithms to achieve maximum image clarity. The development of the Stycast lens presents a promising solution to enhancing detection capabilities without compromising resolution and spectrum sensitivity. Furthermore, this new lens design may also be applied to other sensitive devices, offering them enhanced performance through improved acoustic properties. Overall, this new lens concept provides a feasible alternative to PMMA, allowing for the expansion of the detection area of these devices. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through analyses of synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its ability to yield reliable results and outperform alternative methods. Specifically, our approach outperforms current multi-layer eigenvector centrality methods in identifying key nodes within networks and can be applied to various research fields, such as the study of online communities and social networks. We also provide a suitable resource for computing multi-layer eigenvector centrality values on a central server or distributed environment through a downloadable program.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. The model's ability to generalize to blurring caused by camera movements is also shown through tests. Overall, our approach produces superior results over state-of-the-art methods on public datasets and actual world images. The code and data are available at https://github.com/CannyYang/SRANet.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. In this approach, we first establish the relationship between 
the de Sitter spacetime and the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which allows us to derive the 
$R$-Dirac equation. We subsequently determine the creation and annihilation operators 
within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which are analogous to those within the de Sitter 
spacetime. We then develop a formalism to transform the $R$-Dirac equation into its 
equivalent form within the de Sitter spacetime. This transformation leads to a 
non-hermitian Dirac equation. We propose a new strategy to solve this equation by 
dividing it by a universal factor. We provide explicit expressions for the solutions 
for both non-zero momentum states and zero momentum states, which include both 
particle and anti-particle solutions. We also analyze the energy spectrum and 
propagation length of both particle and anti-particle solutions. We demonstrate that 
both particle and anti-particle solutions exhibit decaying behavior. We attribute 
this decay to an infinite mass correction, which is a consequence of living in a 
curved spacetime. We compare our results with previously derived finite field equation 
by Fring. We also compare our zero momentum state solutions with various previously 
derived solutions, including those by Fukuyama, Fring, and Mignaco et al. We 
discuss how our approach can be extended to the massless case and whether it 
correlates with the Helicity theorem. We propose that our strategy for solving

This study introduces an open source Python framework that utilizes background knowledge and observational data for the purpose of inferring causal relationships. This framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package, which executes a comprehensive causal discovery process to identify the causal interactions and the causal network structure among the variables, drawing from established methodologies including those from 'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg', in addition to pairwise algorithms like ANM. The framework is available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License. A supplemental Jupyter notebook contains illustrations of the framework's functionality and can be found within the repository. A standalone executable installation is also provided. As the framework executes a causal discovery process encompassing the identification of causal interactions and the causal network structure utilizing observational data, it is crucial to appreciate that the accuracy of the inferred causality may be hindered by the presence of noisy data. Consequently, validation of the inferred causality is mandatory through the use of established metrics such as AUC-CAUSAL or the verification of predictions against real world data. A sample observation is showcased in the form of an electronic health record dataset containing 5000 patient entries, where the goal is to establish a causal connection between the diagnosis of a cardiac condition and the levels of physical activity. A Jupyter notebook has been made available to illustrate the utilization of the 'cdt' framework against this dataset. Nevertheless, it is crucial to note that healthcare professionals must interpret the outcomes of the causal discovery process with caution as they relate to individual patient scenarios. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. These findings were obtained through both experimental observations of spheres entering the water's surface at various velocities, and through the analysis of previously conducted research. In the range studied, it is noted that increased velocities generally lead to greater pressures within the cavity, causing more extreme water-entry behaviors, including partial entrapment, partial seal, and partial pinch-off. It is also suggested that the pressure increase results from the enhanced indentation of the water surface by the moving sphere, leading to greater acceleration of water entering the cavity, and supported by both experimental data and potential theory. In the surface-seal regime specifically, it is observed that increased velocities raise the pressure within the cavity to the point where water is squeezed out of the partially sealed cavity, resulting in additional layers of partial seal, until the full pinch-off of the remaining water cavity. It is implied that enhanced pressures within the cavity, caused by increased velocities, lead to the transition from partial seal to full pinch-off, and that this relationship holds across all mid-range speeds. It is also noted that in cases where water is completely pinched off from the cavity, but still in contact with the sphere, further increased velocities may lead to the breaking of this water-layer, no longer considered part of the water-entry interaction, and thus, no longer relevant to the water-entry phenomenon itself. It is suggested that this concept of water-layer-breaking could be a separate collapse regime of water-entry interactions, and that it may occur across all domains of water-entry velocities. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. Furthermore, we found that the range of universal symmetries present in these effective field theories is determined by the complex structure of the corresponding algebraic curve which describes the near-boundary region of the moduli space. Finally, we established that the Calabi-Yau threefolds used in our study contain an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum composed of holomorphic differential forms, which is an outcome of the monodromy transformation, and is an independent element. This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats.

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results showed FPG outperforms the natural policy gradient method and delivers a robust policy with a mere additional computational expense. The source code is available at https://github.com/henryqian/robust-pg. We also introduced a technique for accurately estimating the optimal expected discount reward under reward corruption, which is proportional to the amount of corruption. We provided a theoretical $\ell_2$ regret bound of $O(\epsilon)$ for the filtered policy gradient algorithm, demonstrating its optimal order of complexity. In experiments, the filtered policy gradient method outperformed the natural policy gradient method on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks with reward corruption, achieving a robust policy with minimal additional computational expense. The code is available at https://github.com/henryqian/robust-pg. We also proposed a method to accurately estimate the optimal expected discount reward under corruption, which is directly proportional to the amount of corruption, and derived a theoretical $\ell_2$ regret bound of $O(\epsilon)$ for FPG, demonstrating optimal complexity. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can achieve an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy when the corruption is bounded and established a lower bound of $O(\epsilon)$ for any robust reinforcement learning algorithm. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. By analyzing the crystal field and covalency factors, we explain why certain molecular orbitals are filled with electrons while others are isolated. Additionally, our model explains the relative energies of atomic and molecular orbitals, identifying how the 4t2g atomic orbitals are pushed down in energy while the 5eg atomic orbitals are lifted up. This analysis also allows us to investigate the effects of replacing certain atoms in the cubanite structure, such as substituting zinc for iron in the 4t2g site, which significantly impacts the orbital occupancy and associated energy levels. Lastly, our framework predicts that the unusual orbital behavior in cubanite could lead to other experimental features, such as a redshift in the optical spectrum and a positive optical gap. This study provides a theoretical foundation for a vast class of molecular transition metal compounds, giving insight into their fundamental physics and laying the groundwork for further practical applications. This could potentially result in the discovery of more compounds with desirable properties, such as superconductivity, magnetism, or color, achieved by understanding how to manipulate their orbital structure effectively. This knowledge could also be applied to devices that rely on transition metal ions, such as those involving Mössbauer spectroscopy or X-ray Mössbauer spectroscopy, to accurately simulate their behavior and improve their performance. This work is particularly relevant to materials scientists working with cubanite or similar compounds that contain 3d transition metal ions, such as copper iron oxides, copper zinc ferrites, and zinc iron oxides, and can also be applied to a broader range of molecular transition metal compounds. This study provides a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions in cubanite. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. Furthermore, this advancement raises the possibility of controlling multi-phonon states over time, giving rise to sequential creation of quasi-stationary states comprising distinct phonon bundles and providing a pivotal component for a phonon standard model. Additionally, by adjusting the laser frequency with precision, researchers can switch between absorption and emission of phonon bundles, enabling the direct emission of multi-phonon bundles even in systems with losses, thus demarcating phonon number states over time. A proposed experiment utilizing a semiconductor quantum dot and laser allows for the control of multi-phonon states, creating sequential, quasi-stationary states consisting of distinct phonon bundles, making this a crucial component for a phonon standard model. Moreover, this system enables the direct emission of phonon bundles, enabling the demarcation of phonon number states over time and giving rise to a phonon gun, an instrument that could generate multi-phonon states in sequence, leading to a potential breakthrough in phonon state control. This could have a significant impact on research and development in the field of acoustic physics. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we outline a feasible experimental protocol to generate SPCCSs utilizing linear optical components and coherent pulses, and predict high success probabilities in this scenarios. Ultimately, SPCCSs offer significant potential for applying linear optical catalysis in quantum technology applications.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to obtain the complex coefficients of the electromagnetic field in both Minkowski space basis and complex null tetrad basis. This review aims to provide clear understanding and practical application of bivectors in the context of General Relativity. It is hoped that this will facilitate the discovery of new exact solutions to Einstein's field equations. Additionally, it is intended as a reference for those seeking to expand existing solutions to the gravitational field equations. This will be accomplished by utilizing the symmetry of the solutions to simplify the complex calculations involved. This approach will be illustrated through the example of an expanding, axisymmetric, self-dual gravitational field. The corresponding electromagnetic field will also be determined to ensure physical validity. This study will provide a foundation for a series of investigations into the application of this approach to various types of symmetry in general relativity. It is expected that this approach will lead to innovative breakthroughs in the field of exact solutions to Einstein's field equations. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. A real-field data case was also mimicked to evaluate the method and the results showed similar accuracy as obtained with the synthetic data. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. The code and models are publicly accessible for replication and further research. This is the initial version of this paper, and additional related work on holistic NLP is being incorporated for a comprehensive review. A formal paper is currently under review for publication. We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Additionally, we have developed a data transmission protocol to reduce the location detection data size, making efficient use of limited network memory. This is particularly important as it enables the full location detection process to operate continuously in conjunction with the data transmission protocol. Ultimately, our location detection method has proven capable of accurately determining the location of mobile nodes within the network. 

This work has been previously presented at the 2019 IEEE Workshop on Advances in Sensors and Animations (WASA) held in Tokyo, Japan. This extended version includes the results of a mobile node location detection method developed by ourselves. This method was successfully tested using a ZigBee network and real-world equipment. The location of mobile nodes was accurately determined within a range of up to 5 metres from the base station. A comparison with other location detection methods revealed our approach to be the most precise. A novel method for calculating the distance between nodes was found to significantly reduce location estimation errors. The developed methods have the potential to be applied to other location detection methods.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By acknowledging the disparities in available data, we advocate for a broader range of linguistic resources and tailored models that can handle the unique challenges posed by code-mixing. This position paper also includes best practices for conducting code-mixing research and encourages collaboration among researchers, policymakers, and society to leverage the full potential of NLP. This could yield significant societal gains and address various challenges confronting multilingual communities, encompassing those mentioned above. This work is a initial step towards a more inclusive and dynamic field of code-mixing research and we hope it to contribute to the evolution of this area. This paper is targeted at both researchers and readers who are interested in Code-Mixing with no prior knowledge in this domain. It enumerates and explains various aspects of code-mixing and highlights our research findings. It also offers recommendations for future codemixing research and has been presented at the 13th International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction. It has 26 pages and is available under the CC-BY 4.0 license.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we might assess the ability of descriptions to be understood by other vision systems, which would provide complementary metrics that are less prone to drift than classical methods based on mean squared error. This line of inquiry is particularly relevant given the rapid advancements in image recognition technologies and the scarcity of datasets suitable for such tasks. Visually impaired users' primary concern is understanding descriptions, not how they were generated. Therefore, when designing protocols for data annotation, we should prioritize user interactions that mimic actual description consumption, which is how we should later assess these protocols. As a result, we should use metrics that gauge how well descriptions are comprehended by other vision systems, which will also allow us to take advantage of recent advancements in these areas. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. The studies on Ta$_2$O$_5$ could serve as a model for analyzing other complex materials that exist in multiple forms. Additionally, the techniques used to validate the material's structure through experimental and calculated loss spectra could be applied to additional novel oxides. Ultimately, this approach may provide a way to synthesize the material polymorphs with the best characteristics, leading to better performance in cancer treatment applications. To this end, researchers are exploring ways to produce large quantities of $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ using solution methods. Despite the challenges, studies have demonstrated the potential of Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as enhancers for hadron therapy cancer treatments, and further research may yield significant clinical benefits. To accelerate the development of this approach, there is a need for collaboration between materials scientists and medical professionals. Ultimately, hadron therapy particle separator mirrors, made from Ta$_2$O$_5$, could be a key innovation in the effective treatment of cancer. To move forward with this goal, it is essential to prioritize the scientific studies required to validate the material's properties and engage with the cancer treatment community to inform and guide the development process. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, in areas where residents value organization and planning, we found increased circulation of organizational content, including misinformation, presented in a structured manner. Our findings have implications for the development of strategies to tackle online misinformation, and we discuss potential approaches to tailor misinformation mitigation to diverse cultural and population contexts. We also introduce the Concept Awareness Store (CAS), a theoretical framework for monitoring public concept usage, and present Reddit as a large-scale test bed for this idea. By leveraging existing knowledge graphs, we can identify concepts whose increase in public usage anticipates changes in online circulation, including the emergence of new concepts, such as events, and the decline of existing ones. We applied the CAS framework to analyze the dynamics of public concept usage in relation to online misinformation dissemination. We found that the rise of misinformation was often linked to the growth of subcommunities and the increase in user population in certain states. Moreover, we identified bridges between the digital and physical worlds, including the influence of local personality traits and cultural characteristics on online misinformation dissemination. We also discovered instances of concurrent public concept usage increases in offline events and online content circulation, such as the rise of anti-fluoride movements and videos promoting the opposite agenda. Our research expands the study of online misinformation spread, highlighting the significance of geographical and cultural factors, and introducing the Concept Awareness Store (CAS) framework for monitoring public concept usage and online circulation in parallel dimensions. We have made our data set and analysis code publicly available to facilitate further research in this area. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code and data used in this research are openly available, providing a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to create comparable systems. Furthermore, we highlight key challenges and potential research directions for further improvement and exploration. HALFADO's efficient detection capability, combined with its efficiency and transparency, makes it an excellent foundation for actionable data streams and human-augmented machine learning systems. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our results suggest that incorporating auditory feedback into robotic training could lead to improved performance in tasks where visual feedback is limited or misleading. To facilitate progress in this area, our research provides a auditory feedback dataset along with a preliminary framework for analysis, which can be building blocks for future developments. Additionally, possible directions for enhancing robotic learning through auditory feedback in scenarios mimicking real-world environments are also explored. This work has the potential to contribute to more efficient and effective robotic learning from demonstrations combined with audio feedback from human instructors. In addition, it may also benefit other research areas involving humans and their auditory environments. In order to facilitate progress in this area, we are sharing our initial analysis, along with a proposed framework, and a newly created dataset called Auditory Demo Data (ADD), which is now publicly available to advance research in this area. Ultimately, uncovering the content and value of audio feedback in human-robot learning interactions may lead to a combined approach that efficiently blends demonstration-based learning with instruction-based learning. This could help address challenges posed by complex, real-world environments requiring a collaboration between humans and robots. In such scenarios, humans and robots may need to cooperate on managing shared resources, navigating multi-agent environments, and adapting to new task requirements.
