One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our code is available at https://github.com/araoumar/fc2il. Lastly, we contribute a diversity of corrective feedback types that can be used in conjunction with popular online learning algorithms, capable of handling different forms of noisy feedback, thereby enriching the IL field's toolbox. This enrichment empowers researchers to embark on new challenges at the intersection of IL and online learning. This work lays the groundwork for exploring a variety of feedback types in various learning settings and encourages the community to contribute to this diverse pool of corrective feedback types, thus enriching the field's capabilities even further. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory and the relationship between infinite combinatorial principles in the context of Robinson's theory. Notably, we examine how the Continuum problem's solution or nonsolution affects the characterization of model companions for set theory, and analyze the implications of this relationship for infinite combinatorial principles. Additionally, we outline a strategy to bypass dependence on the Continuum problem's solution or nonsolution. This strategy involves constructing a maximal model companion for set theory that is equivalent to adding an infinite number of distinct combinatorial principles to $ZFC$. One of these principles is $\square_\kappa$, under the condition that $2^\kappa=\kappa^+$ holds. This research draws upon a previously developed method, applying a technique suggested by Hodges in 'Building Model Theory'. This approach involves using a strong theory's model companion to enhance a weaker theory, resulting in a strengthened model companion. This process is demonstrated with the infinitary logic $L_{\omega_1,\omega}$, which surpasses $L_{\omega_1,\omega*}$, a fragment of first-order logic that includes the quantifier $\square_\kappa$. This research's conclusions regarding the relationship between infinite combinatorial principles and model companions for set theory or its extensions address open questions initially posed by R. Layton. This work is also a representation of the higher-set-theory extensions of Hodges' method, which provides a framework for constructing model companions across various set-theoretic contexts. This framework allows for the generation of a wide array of model companions in contexts supported by heavy combinatorial evidence but lacks sufficient axioms. An auxiliary article presents the foundational proof techniques necessary for this research within the context of $L_{\omega_1,\omega}$. This research is further expanded upon in the companion papers 'Building Model Theory in Second-Order Arithmetic I' and 'II'. The resulting model companions for set theory or its extensions comprise the strongest possible theories within a specific class, characterized by their relationship with infinite combinatorial principles. This relationship between a theory and its model companion holds the potential to provide insights into the nature of the Continuum problem. Notably, if the Continuum problem has a solution, it will be found within the model companion for $\aleph_2$. Chan's equation variant includes an extra differential operator and matches the Branson-Paneitz equation when this extra operator is zero. To demonstrate the existence of a weak solution, this work employs a combination of the compactness method and an argument based on the induced gradient flow structure. Additionally, this research includes an analysis of an associated energy functional and proves that it satisfies optimal regularity conditions under certain strict stability assumptions. Finally, this research investigates its implications in a periodic boundary context. This research expands on previous results from R. S. W. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our work represents a significant advancement in the realm of everyday commonsense knowledge and its application in enhancing natural language understanding.  This is reflected in our having created extensive networks of semantic relationships and a comprehensive suite of evaluation tools that can produce human-rated evaluation data.  Our dataset, along with your interest, can spark further development in this area, ensuring that machines equipped with this knowledge will better navigate the complexities of human language and behavior.  This knowledge is now readily available at https://www.atomicdata.org.  In parallel with this dataset, we have launched a related web platform that allows users to browse through the defined relationships and evaluate the underlying conditions that give rise to these relationships, with all of this knowledge and this evaluation data being fully extensible by machine learning models themselves.  This is with the goal of creating a dynamic atlas of everyday commonsense knowledge that is both rich in content and continuously learning and adaptable in the face of new information.  Ultimately, this represents a fundamental shift in the direction of NLP, where machines are no longer confined to solely processing text but now also have a deep understanding of the underlying causal relationships that give rise to this text, enabling them to engage with human language and behavior in a more comprehensive and meaningful way. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. As such, it offers an adaptable framework for developers to exploit the capabilities of new NISQ devices for applications involving end-to-end quantum execution. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This technique also proves successful on the Google Speech dataset, resulting in a 12.7% decrease in word error rate with only paired data and as much as 2.4% when additional unpaired text is incorporated. This indicates that multi-modal training is a valuable technique for improving the efficiency of ASR models. Additionally, the results show substantial improvements over alternative multi-modal learning approaches. This technique is compatible with various transformer-based ASR models, including Transformer, Transformer-ASR, and Dual-Flow Transformer. This leads to further advancements in speech-environment specific sauce, allowing ASR to effectively employ unpaired text data for pretraining, which may be paired with environmental information to enhance speech representations even more. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating the system to be older than 1 billion years, and also identified high CO molecular abundance replicating earlier observations, which provide implications for this object's formation and evolution, further contributing to the knowledge of analyzing brown dwarfs and planets through new-generation telescopes. Additionally, a re-examination of the mass-based evidence supporting GJ 229B's orbital path revealed no support, instead suggesting a potential shared disk or interactions with a second companion. Lastly, we propose that ongoing and future surveys, such asrow~II, should prioritize follow-up analysis of discovered T-dwarfs, such as 2MASS 1509-—a newly identified T-dwarf companion that warrants further examination.

As a result, our findings provide valuable guidelines for optimizing the functioning of these complex photonic structures. We anticipate that this technology will play a significant part in the future evolution of applications such as quantum communications, biometric data processing and global environmental monitoring. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Moreover, we've established a connection between unclonable encryption and quantum one-way functions, presenting a new paradigm for analyzing such functions. By exploring this connection, we've a question whether the existence of quantum one-way functions is necessary for unclonable encryption, leaving this inquiry for future research. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for further investigation into the concepts of unclonable encryption and its various implications.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission with negligible
efficiency loss, providing an attacker's knowledge does not equate to total access.
Notably, this technique does not rely on the specific characteristics of an attacker's
transmission and does not require a shared secret, thereby facilitating the
implementation of a secure and robust communication system. Furthermore, a secure
transmission capacity model was formulated and found to converge to standard
transmission capacity when no unauthorized access occurs. As a modular system,
this approach can be applied across multiple scenarios. Moreover, a low-cutoff
frequency version of this model was analyzed to assess its convergence to well-known
models, including the full-duplex model and the half-duplex model, under various
adversarial access conditions. As a model-based approach, this technique can
be utilized in optimization tools and communication protocol design. As such, it
represents a crucial development, with potential applications in various scenarios.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials. 

This study is published in Phys. Rev. B 107, 125403 (2023).

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It focuses particularly on the external interactions
between planets and their surrounding wind flow, including the potential impacts on
the search for extraterrestrial life. It also discusses the related observational
and theoretical research areas. It is essential to note that the physics of these
planetary interactions are in the early stages of being explored, and numerous
unsolved problems remain in this field. It is hoped that this review will help
identify key aspects worthy of in-depth investigation. It is based on previous
research and recent findings, including those obtained through the author's
participation in the Zanita 2.0 model development, a new version of the solar
radiative wind model, which can be applied to different types of stars. It is
essential to test this model across a broad spectrum of stellar types, especially
those with variable masses, as well as in planetary scenarios, to thoroughly
understand these complex celestial interactions. It is anticipated that advancing
this research will reveal new phenomena and shed light on many as yet
unexplained observations. It is hoped that this review will serve as a foundation
for a comprehensive theoretical model that can be applied across both stellar and
planetary contexts. It is the author's intention to make the Zanita 2.0 model, as
well as the new solar model, publicly available for scientific use and review.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We also found that our method prevents the formation of edges with zero weights, leading to improved activation pattern diversity and a reduction in over-fitting. We believe that exploring this approach may lead to a greater understanding of neural network training and its relationship with continuity constraints. We have made our method's Python implementation available as part of the Neural Tangent Kernel suite. 

This work has been accepted for publication at the 25th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistical Modeling.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
With combined data from two agreement prediction tasks, we outline our tactics
for preprocessing and normalizing the data, presenting a set of challenging
experiments to validate the language-learning capabilities of neural network models. 
Their performance is analyzed in both sequential and pseudo-cyclic configurations
with and without sentence context, resulting in reliable data suitable for
benchmarking a range of NLP models. 
We make the code, model performances, and the data used in this research
available online at this link https://github.com/ali213/basque-agreement-benchmark. 
Ultimately, our objectives involve equipping researchers with diagnostic tools
for assessing a language model's comprehension of hierarchical sentence structures
and providing a rigorous framework for testing a neural network's language-learning
abilities in the complex and systematically irregular Basque language context.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to detect subtle irregularities in the planet's orbit when combined with upcoming observations using the James Webb Space Telescope. This enhanced precision is particularly important because it is critical to compare the planet's internal and orbital periods if it is to be considered for tests of gravitational physics at the smallest scales. This new data, along with new analyses of the planet's atmosphere, is set to significantly impact the ongoing studies of HD80606b in the coming years. This project is also an opportunity to showcase the capabilities of international collaborative research through this public report. This document is intended for a broad scientific audience and includes key findings related to HD80606b's orbit, as well as the methodology used to obtain this data, and the wider implications for the planet and future related research. This work is an offshoot of the Eyes Open Exoplanets Project, a global network of small telescopes that is used to study a range of exoplanetary phenomena through direct imaging, transits, radial velocity, and stellar activity indicators. This project is part of the Eyes Open Exoplanets Project's efforts to contribute to the most significant scientific projects involving direct detection missions such as Plato and EChO. This work is an example of how global networks of small and medium-sized telescopes can make meaningful contributions to major scientific projects involving direct detection missions such as Plato and EChO. Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. This approach could also be adapted for other applications where a system's performance is shaped by both human input and automated processes, leading to new insights into the dynamics of human-machine interactions. This research was presented at the 13th International Conference on Advances in Computer Entertainment technology in 2011.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. Specifically, we focus on a periodic, bounded domain where multiple, non-overlapping regions represent solid substrates, a common scenario in biological and soft matter sciences. To capture these structures, we use a piecewise-standard form to represent the approximation, and it has been demonstrated that it converges to a suitable limit when the mesh size approaches zero. Our approach has the benefit of providing computationally tractable models while still reflecting the fundamental mechanics underlying brittle fracture in rigid solids. Consequently, this model can be employed to model adiabatic compressive treatment procedures, resulting in computationally efficient algorithms that yield physically plausible results. As part of the model's development, we also established a regularized formulation and obtained its compactness property, which enables us to define a suitable energy space for the problem. Ultimately, our strategy can be extended to accommodate multiphase structures and gradually removes the rigidity assumption as the mesh size decreases, yielding a more realistic model of fracture in composite materials. This research has been reflected in an existing simulation, with corresponding data available, and it offers a promising framework for further investigation into fracture-related problems across a broad spectrum of applications.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of ditau events to reveal the existence of vector leptoquarks if their mass is within the range of approximately 350 to 450 GeV unless their production mechanism significantly limits their detection. Additionally, this code can be adapted for extensions to the standard model beyond the scope of this specific research. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Furthermore, compared to existing deep learning approaches, this novel framework demonstrates a marked improvement in robustness when processing OOD data, as indicated by a significant reduction in negative log likelihood values. This uncertainty-aware neural network is now available on an open-source platform. Nonetheless, most current datasets are not sufficient to evaluate the proposed framework's performance fully, so we encourage researchers to contribute their own OOD PET-MRI acquisitions to facilitate further development and testing of this innovative technology. The code can be found at https://github.com/CRAO-UofA/UncAwarePET, with the accompanying data featured in the results being hosted at https://data.talia.org/search/dataset/62f4b5b5d5b3e21d2d5b5b5b. Growing worries about over-collected data and its unintended use have motivated our research on balancing personalization and privacy. Our experience creating personalized content platforms that protect users' confidentiality has sparked an investigation into users' attitudes towards these topics. A conducted survey revealed the opinions of various age groups regarding personalization and privacy. In this research, we are sharing our key discoveries with publishers and the community to inform the design and development of next-generation news recommender systems, which should prioritize the human user and achieve a harmonious balance between personalization and privacy. Our findings have important implications for the ongoing evolution of personalized content platforms. Furthermore, our results include practical recommendations for system designers and operators aiming to implement transparent, user-centric data processing methods. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The implications of these findings are also considered. The methods and data used in the study are also discussed in detail. The study employs a method that searches for the most connected statement in the text and incorporates various features that have been previously used to recognize connections within the text. The study is conducted using a large dataset of written texts known as the Discourse Comprehension Corpus. The study's findings are validated through additional experiments conducted on separate subsets of the dataset. The study's theory and methods are also considered in the context of how they relate to CT and other approaches to analyzing connections within the text, as well as the systems that recognize these connections. The study's results have aspects that can inform the development of computer systems that are capable of understanding the connections within the text, especially in written texts. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Our research contributes new insights to the study of directed graphs' embeddability in an upward planar layout. Moreover, our findings provide new bounds for directed graph parameters and introduce new methods for detecting substructures within directed graphs. Our research is showcased through interactive demonstrations of our algorithmic results and underlying theories. Our code is openly accessible and can be utilized for our method implementations. The rising intricacy of modern adaptable systems demands elevated automation in their configuration process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated workflow integration. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved human understanding via metric-driven optimization. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to configuring a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks. The introduced approach boosts automation capability in memory tile configuration by up to 15 times, compared to the same-sized related study. The advanced framework and its evaluation are available online.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Ultimately, our work demonstrates the operator growth hypothesis's universality across Lie-symmetric systems, while also highlighting the significance of employing quantum information theory as a tool for analyzing complex operator dynamics.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. To evaluate the generalizability of the models, cross-validation was performed on multiple datasets that were not part of the training data. A widely applicable model was proposed utilizing a combination of signal distance metrics and genetic feature selection, and this approach was found to outperform other scenarios according to evolutionary optimization. To make this approach accessible to researchers without machine learning expertise, a user-friendly web application was developed and is available online at https://wifi.gunjan.com/. To further enhance this research, the associated dataset, featuring 1240 data sets from 13 sources, is being made available for additional analysis and improvement of the model. To facilitate progress in this area, the researchers also established a challenges page on the project website, outlining potential areas for improvement and related problems. To contribute to this research, a GitHub repository has been set up at the following address: https://github.com/gunjanbhay/Generalized-WiFi-Feature-Selection. To move forward, the researchers invite feedback, suggestions, and improvements to this approach and the associated dataset. Consequently, this innovative machine learning approach for geospatial data extraction from WiFi fingerprints may pave the way for the development of robust, location-independent positioning algorithms that can effectively employ any suitable signal distance metric. For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres. With many black holes similar to GW311040853 having suitable conditions for a Dyson Sphere, existence probabilities can be refined with astrophysical constraints. Ultimately, a comprehensive strategy is proposed to locate and study these artificial structures more effectively. By focusing on suitable black hole hosts and observing multiple candidate targets, the sensitivity of current telescopes can be fully utilized in searching for signs of extraterrestrial life. A simplified model predicting detectability and existence probability thresholds can guide researchers in identifying the most promising candidates for further analysis. With an expected one thousand suitable black holes hosting Dyson Spheres in the Milky Way galaxy, a comprehensive study of these artificial structures is only accessible with a systematic observational approach. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the identification of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering active measurement tools via P2P. These principles involve autonomous decision-making across a network via a self-regulating system. Subsequently, we outline strategies for activating measurement sessions that are based on these principles, which do not need human input, can adapt to alterations in network conditions, and operate independently of underlying active measurement technologies. Finally, we examine the potential applications of this approach, which could see a more active role for end devices, more efficient use of measurement resources, and new types of active measurement tools. Nonetheless, several challenges must be addressed before the features we describe can be implemented effectively. These challenges include defining relevant measurement criteria, managing data conflicts, handling network dynamics, ensuring secure participation, and addressing scalability issues. Ultimately, we believe that the integration of P2P technology and active measurement systems could give rise to dynamic, adaptable, and autonomous network management systems, which are crucial for the effective provision of SLAs in next-generation networks. Moreover, this approach has the potential to be applicable across a broad spectrum of network contexts, ranging from wireless sensor networks to cellular networks, and could contribute to the development of self-managing networks via the integration of P2P and other relevant technologies. Despite the various challenges it poses, further exploration of this concept is warranted. This is because the features we describe could give rise to innovative active measurement techniques, promote the efficient use of measurement resources, enable more effective identification of SLA breaches, and facilitate a greater understanding of network dynamics, which is critical for the provision of high-quality services and applications. This article provides a foundation for this area of research, which is on the cusp of a paradigm shift, and is therefore in need of further in-depth study. This could yield significant advantages, which could be realized through the development of cutting-edge active measurement tools, the effective detection of SLA breaches, and a deeper understanding of network dynamics, all of which are critical for the provision of excellent services and applications

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In fact, with appropriately chosen filling patterns, the beam breakup instability barrier can be increased to levels achievable by other stability preservation methods. This concept is demonstrated through simulation data from a generic future light source, showing how the appropriate selection of filling patterns can postpone the onset of beam breakup by several factors. Furthermore, this approach is seen to raise the beam current threshold by a factor of almost 30, nearly matching the levels produced by finite natural cavity cutoffs. Ultimately, this study suggests that careful design of filling patterns can provide a simple and effective means of conquering beam breakup instability in future energy recovery linacs. This approach is scheduled for testing at the MAX IV 3 GeV ring, due for commissioning in 2023. Until then, the full impact of its potential cannot be fully assessed. This work is part of on-going research aimed at exploring design options for multi-pass energy recovery linacs that can function reliably without beam breakup instability mitigation. This goal is now within reach for energy recovery linacs with beam temperatures below 1.5 degrees Kelvin and beam current thresholds above 10 Ampere, providing scope for additional uses of these machines. This new design dimension, made possible by recent superconductivity breakthroughs, is set to be tested at the 3 GeV ring of the MAX IV synchrotron in Lund, due for commissioning in 2023. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The most compelling finding was the observation of neutral particle events with energies exceeding 200 MeV for the first time, yielding event samples of 36 and 46 for 2019 and 2020, respectively. The implementation of a machine learning algorithm for event selection resulted in a reduction of background contamination from 11.5 to 5.5% at 500 MeV. The results from these prototype developments have validated the design concepts for the long-baseline neutrino detection systems in the ECL/MWPA project. Nonetheless, a significant margin exists between the detection capabilities achieved through these prototype research and the actual requirements needed for accurate neutrino energy reconstruction in real-scale experiments. Therefore, further development along with upgraded neutron detection technologies will be necessary to fulfill the requirements for next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments. The outcomes of the research conducted with these prototypes have been presented along with the implications for the design and operation of real-scale long-baseline neutrino detection systems. The findings from the 2019 and 2020 neutron irradiation experiments have been combined into a single data set for the purpose of developing refined models of neutrino-nucleus interactions through the application of genetic neural networks. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth. In addition, we observed stickier dry samples by means of thermal desorption in the cooler sections of the discs, which may result in a greater likelihood of collisions among particles in these areas, leading to faster growth and ultimately giving rise to larger planetary bodies that can sustain massive gravitational influence over surrounding materials during later stages of planetary development. In the case of temperatures of up to 1000 K, our study supports existing evidence as it indicates aggregate growth becomes stuck at some point, which may result in a population of smaller bodies. In addition, our study provides a new framework for calculating the likelihood of collisions among particles by taking into account the increased sticking forces at higher temperatures, which may have far-reaching implications for our existing models of planetary development. In addition, we believe our study may have implications for a broader range of topics related to the development of planetary systems. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Moreover, LFDA is compatible with classification algorithms like k-Nearest Neighbors (knn) to evaluate the efficacy of reduced data. The package includes a range of options for the localization function, including distance metrics (Euclidean, Manhattan, Correlation) and regression types (Linear, Logistic). The package's recent updates include RBGLocAF, for localized t-Distributed Vector Analysis, and a new implementation for LFDA. The package is available on CRAN and can be sourced from the GitHub repository. Additionally, comprehensive documentation is provided on the package's website. Numerous example datasets are included to illustrate the package's applications. LFDA is an open-source and community-driven project, encouraging users to report issues and contribute new features.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://github.com/robotics-irving/EKMP. Our research offers a novel solution for conforming robot skill learning to complex tasks and can serve as a foundation for future works combining imitation learning and motion planning.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In contrast, under NMRK kinematic limits, distinct connections between conformally invariant cross ratios and trajectory functions emerge. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the two-gluon CEV, defined at NMRK limits, corresponds to specific trajectory function configurations in both N=4 SYM theory and QCD, showcasing the relationship between conformally invariant cross ratios and trajectory functions under these constraints. In addition, various anomalous dimensions associated with conformally invariant cross ratios have been calculated to NNLL accuracy in both theories. Lastly, various six-gluon amplitude calculations, involving jet functions and soft function in deeply inelastic scattering processes, have been re-examined, yielding improved accuracy. In particular, corrections to the BFKL kernel, impact factors, colour-singlet distribution amplitude, and the two-glue impact factor, all evaluated at NNLL accuracy, reveal significant discrepancies with existing literature in certain cases. In contrast, the NNLL-bounded colour-singlet soft function, defined through conformal bootstrap methods and independent of trajectory functions, exhibits full convergence at NNLL accuracy in both theories. Moreover, various observable calculations, including DIS differential cross sections, revealed various shifts, primarily attributed to NNLL-bounded trajectory functions, leading to further validation of the derived results. Lastly, various generalised six-gluon amplitude configurations, defined through cross ratios in both N=4 SYM theory and QCD, have been shown

Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Lastly, we discuss potential experimental realizations of this non-Abelian physics using helical electron materials such as InSb or InAs, suggesting that careful adjustment of Rashba coupling and Zeeman field strength may be feasible through applied magnetic field manipulation. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The starting point of this rotation state in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ can be adjusted by changing the doping concentration $x$, and it appears that it occurs only when the doping concentration is very close to the critical point $x=p=0.17$. 

This finding proves that the interlocked vortex lattice in this material can rotate when subjected to intense magnetic fields, a phenomenon that can provide further insight into the nature of this material's superconducting properties. The discovered transition can also be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, and it reveals a complex and intricate picture of this material's behavior in such conditions. 

Finally, our study shows that the rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees can be adjusted by changing the doping concentration $x$, and it appears that it only occurs when the doping concentration is very close to the critical point $x=p=0.17$. This finding is significant because it provides further evidence for the $d$-wave nature of superconductivity in this material, and it highlights the importance of studying the interlocked vortex lattice in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ at high magnetic fields and low temperatures. 

In addition, our study has implications for the broader field of superconductivity research, and it may lead to a greater understanding of the complex and intricate behavior of interlocked vortices in superconductors. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. In fact, we've already successfully utilized this approach in analyzing the morphology of a notable herringbone structure. This research advances our theoretical understanding of stretched brush geometry and free energy calculations, crossing the limit of small and large radii of curvature, and offers a flexible tool for predicting brush properties in complex situations. It may also serve as a general framework for investigating other surface-confined melts and solids in the molten state. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some well-known graphs like a straight line, a cycle, a tree and a complete graph have already had their beta_k determined but some others like the cube and the tetrahedral graph have not. Additionally, we discovered that beta_2 of these graphs is 2, and that this is the minimum identifying set that does it. A method of finding metric dimension in graphs is also discussed using a technique called the cut method. Finally, some research is suggested on graphs that are not planar.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method could be adapted to other imaging satellites, like those being proposed for the Imaging X-Gamma Ray All-Sky Survey, which will be capable of producing an incredibly large number of maps per year. To realize this, future studies need to address challenges with source confusion, large fields of view, and a possible shorter exposure time. Nonetheless, this investigation indicates that machine learning can revolutionize the analysis of all-sky maps, making it possible to study important astronomical sources and phenomena that were previously difficult to capture with, or be detected from, the data available at that time. This research was based on publicly available Fermi data and was conducted in collaboration with the IMAGINE Project. The associated code and results have been shared with the community to stimulate feedback and advancements in this area. The findings mentioned in this paper are largely a byproduct of a larger analysis aimed at identifying giant structures and studying the galactic diffuse emission emensity in the gamma-ray range. Those specific findings are not detailed in this study. Instead, it highlights the value of machine learning in enhancing image quality and discovering transient sources, demonstrating a novel approach that is certain to be useful in future all-sky surveys. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We conclude that action sequences are a viable method for addressing various combinatorial optimization challenges. Additionally, we introduce and experiment with a new query-based approach that maximizes fractional values in a matrix game scenario, also achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to certain optimization tasks, albeit with little practical value due to its generation of unrealistic action sequences. We conclude that action sequences can effectively address various combinatorial optimization challenges. We offer our code online for public review at https://github.com/ram10909/SD-with-a-view.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Of the 4149 reviewed images, our analysis identified 139 targets for 
follow-up, including 10 existing documented binary asteroids. Ultimately, our 
research identified 3 confirmed wide binary asteroids, and 1 candidate. This 
research is shared in the form of a publicly accessible database featuring 
detected binary prospects along with associated targets for further observation. 
The full dataset is now incorporated into the Secostats2 database accessible at
https://costast2.ipac.caltech.edu/BinaryAsteroids/. The included paper has been
posted to the Pan-STARRS1 website and cited as PS1-20210201. The discovery of
wide binary asteroids relies heavily on the data provided by wide field surveys
like the one undertaken in this research, and future studies are expected to
yield additional findings thanks in part to the methodology presented here. The
analytical approach outlined in this research may also be applied to the
analysis of other extended objects within wide field images. The methodology
described can be located in the paper appended to this research, and titled "A
Primer on the Analysis of Wide Binary Asteroids". The methods discussed within
this research are anticipated to be useful in the analysis of additional wide
field surveys, including those conducted by the LSST. The approach outlined
here may also be applied to the examination of other wide binary objects
beyond those in the solar system.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established. These formulas provide clear connections between fractions of different orders, demonstrating their interconnectedness. Further, this research proves a product rule formula for a combination of variable and constant order operators. Ultimately, this work aims to expand the applicability of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional differential operator to a broader class of functions, including polynomials, exhibiting their surjectivity in the space of real numbers. This development is accompanied by an illustration of a minimal solution to a stochastic variable-order differential equation, indicating the efficacy of the method. Ultimately, this approach is anticipated to benefit the study of fractional differential equations. The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in sedimentary pattern cross-correlations between West Africa and Brazil, particularly in the distribution of deltaic and source rock sediments.  This research has significant implications for hydrocarbon exploration, particularly in understanding depositional history and generating conducive environments for oil and gas accumulation.  It also highlights the extensional reactivation of pre-existing fractures and fault lines, leading to the formation of prominent N-S trending rift- and sag-basin structures, and influenced conjugate margin geometry and relative sea-floor area changes.  These features, in turn, controlled stratal patterns, sedimentary flow, and the development of sedimentary basins.  This study demonstrates the extension of the concept of velocity ratio asymmetry to intra-continental rifts, providing a possible explanation for the origin of the S~ao Paulo High, an area of thinned and extended crust, located in the axis of the E-W directed pre-breakup extension.  This led to its relative subsidence during breakup and resulting in a relative high in stratal patterns, contributing to favorable conditions for oil and gas accumulation.  This model for the development of the South Atlantic conjugate margins may be applied to other intra-plate rifts and developing supercontinents.

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images. 
Notably, our method achieves a notable reduction in codebook size while
maintaining competitive performance.  Moreover, codebook learning via unsupervised
segmentation results in a more compact codebook with improved generalizability. 
In contrast, conventional contrastive learning techniques often rely on rigid
positivematching, leading to a less compact codebook with limited generalization. 
Our approach has been made open-source, and is available for download at 
https://github/lingroup/LAMENT-SFA. 
Our code has been successfully integrated into the MIMAgenerator, a tool 
developed by the PASCAL Visual Interaction Challenge 2020 organizers, 
facilitating the easy generation of unsupervised segmentation datasets. 
This code has also been incorporated into the DeepGAtor framework, 
along with other advanced medical image processing techniques. 
In particular, it includes a robust codebase that encompasses a variety 
of cutting-edge applications, such as image registration, segmentation, 
masking, and generative models, all built with PyTorch and TRACER. 
This codebase is available for download at
