We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we observed notable enhancements in the players' learning abilities as well as an enriched experience for themselves. The code has been made publicly accessible for replication purposes. Additional information is accessible via https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06218 for thorough replication details.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. For instance, utilizing both methodologies, we uncovered 'Atemlos' - a German word whose meaning evolved from initially referring to breathingless anxiety to its current interpretation of breathless excitement. Further development and enhancement of this framework are intended to facilitate ongoing discussion within the field. It is accessible at https://github.com/fkahnemann/DiscoverySuite, facilitating the discovery of new words with changing meanings.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This statistical approach can be applied to various types of protein knots, providing a detailed look at the folding processes in proteins with complex structures. For example, it is observed that proteins with knots in the '8a' type fold quickly, while those with '4a' type knots require more time. Notably, this research reveals that proteins with knots in the '8a' type have a high tendency to be misfolded and that improving their folding efficiency could lead to several beneficial outcomes, such as enhanced stability and reduced aggregation. Overall, this approach offers a novel framework for analyzing protein geometry and folding, which can be modified to study other proteins by adjusting the focus and applying the same statistical methods. For instance, when studying ribonucleoprotein complexes, this approach can be adapted to analyze not just protein geometry but also RNA geometry, or a combination of both, to investigate how they interact and influence each other. By leveraging this approach, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between protein geometry, folding, and interaction with other molecules. Furthermore, this framework can be utilized to identify various protein families that have not been categorized before. For instance, it has been identified that about one-fifth of proteins with knots in the '8a' type have double-loop structures similar to trefoil knots. Additionally, this research reveals distinct folding patterns for proteins with knots other than trefoil knots when comparing folded and unfolded states. Interestingly, when comparing the folded and unfolded states of proteins with trefoil knots, no significant differences were found. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Notably, this analysis ignores variations in EDE's onset and duration, treating them as secondary factors that can be further explored in more comprehensive models. Nonetheless, our simplified approach yields significant insights into EDE's fundamental characteristics. Additionally, we investigated how best to interpret existing EDE limits through a re-analysis of various datasets, incorporating a statistical test to differentiate genuine EDE signals from biased parameter estimates. Ultimately, our study suggests a more comprehensive re-examination of EDE by considering a wider range of parameters in simulations and accounting for secondary factors that influence its behavior within the cosmos.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. A new perspective is offered on previous work related to the anomalous NG theorem, and the necessary mathematical frameworks for Lie algebras and geometry have been reviewed with an emphasis on their relevance to this phenomenon. Theoretical models associated with the anomalous NG theorem have been re-examined in the context of this review, and several novel algebraic structures related to the Lie algebra symmetry breaking have been identified. A discussion on the potential observational evidence for the anomalous NG theorem has been undertaken, and some open questions have been posed in this review's concluding section. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code and data produced within this research are currently available at https://github.com/google-research/disco-cf.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This study provides theoretical insights with first-principles total energy calculations to better understand the interactions between different surfaces of the Heusler compounds and graphene, demonstrating that the most stable configurations are those with epitaxial relationships or rotation domains, depending on the particular system. This work sets the stage for exploring remote epitaxy with a variety of materials and surfaces, including semiconductors and metals. It also suggests that growing films at lower temperatures could significantly increase the likelihood of obtaining remote epitaxy. The method presented here offers a powerful approach for developing a new generation of heterostructures with controlled rotation domains, necessary for enhancing device performance in fields such as spintronics and optoelectronics. It also provides an innovative way to grow bulk Heusler compounds with preferred orientations, essential for enhancing their magnetic or thermal properties. This approach has the potential to expand the application scope of remote epitaxy to a wide range of materials and surfaces. It's now possible to grow films with desired properties, not limited to spintronics and thermoelectric applications, and could also benefit sectors such as energy, catalysis, and sensors. The unique 30 degree rotated superstructure observed in this study may serve as a reference for identifying remote epitaxy in the future. The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs. Furthermore, a technical specification for
graded polymer floods has been proposed and its feasibility examined through simulation. Finally,
a discussion on implementation challenges and potential issues has been presented, along with
 suggestions for addressing them through further research and testing. GVF-1, a computer program,
has been introduced and demonstrated to be an efficient tool for evaluating polymer flooding
strategies. However, this program only provides results for specific polymer distributions and
cannot be utilized for real-time decision-making. In contrast, a more complex simulation program,
IPRS, has been developed for managing polymer flooding operations, although its capacity to
accurately model polymer flooding has yet to be validated. Ultimately, collaboration among
industry practitioners, researchers, and government agencies is seen as crucial for overcoming
the challenges associated with efficient polymer flooding technology. A potential collaborative
pathway is proposed, involving joint experimentation, data analysis, and simulation modeling.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels. A novel single-positive GAN model is proposed to learn from single-positive samples and leverage the remaining unlabelled data to enhance performance. Experimental results show that this model can effectively learn from single-positive datasets and surpass traditional GAN models when working with real-world data sets, such as images. Moreover, the model's ability to handle multiple conditions is demonstrated using synthetic data, and its ability to learn from single-positive datasets is analyzed in detail. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zwang84/Single-Positive-Conditional-GAN. The paper has been accepted for publication in the 2021 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. It is only when the state is cyclic and irreducible that the abstract relationship becomes an actual adjoint pair of maps, thereby yielding an abstract symmetry between the algebra and its representation in this specific circumstance. This finding is closely related to the principles of quantum symmetry encountered in the context of the WZW fusion problem. Ultimately, this analysis yields a new perspective on the famous Haag's theorem from particle physics, often interpreted as demonstrating the failure of the WEP in this field. This perspective, however, suggests that the underlying mathematical structure actually captures the inherent reasons for which the algebra and the representation can never achieve a perfect, strong adjoint relationship in this domain. Instead, the abstract relationship can only behave as an adjoint one generalised to categories of functors. This specific feature of the algebra's representation is what gives rise to the phenomenon of particle scattering. It is through the changed unitary operator obtained after applying the abstract inverse construction that the system's initial and final states become connected. This unitary operator contains all the relevant information about the particle's scattering behaviour. Consequently, implementing this understanding through interferometry enables the direct detection of the abstract algebra that underlies the physical world. It demonstrates that the abstract collection of physical observables associated with a particle has a direct, tangible impact on the particle's behaviour in the laboratory setting. It is only when we are observing the particle in multiple channels at once, effectively performing the abstract construction in reverse, that this abstract collection of observables manifests as a physical, non-unitary operator that cannot be replicated locally. This is the fundamental reason for particle interference and, more broadly, for the inherent non-locality that underlies the physical world. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. The code for our methods is available online and ready for use in practical applications.

After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17]. It further broadens the framework first introduced in [16], which addressed continuous control issues. It is also interesting to note that some of our techniques yield novel insights and simpler proofs for certain cases. Lastly, it is worthwhile to mention that one of our main results can be applied to analyze a model of best of N competition, where the winners engage in a continuous arm race. It is possible to find an optimal strategy when N is any finite number. It is also possible to establish the existence and uniqueness of strategies when N is infinite, under a specific scaling, whose limits are related to a system of stochastic differential equations that includes a system of interacting player systems of Cuckerman and Pignounat. It is also demonstrated that the optimal cost function for the finite N case, when costs for switching are zero, exhibits a periodic structure, while for the infinite N case, it exhibits a non-ergodic behavior, where its averages converge to a different value, as proven through numerical simulations. To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints. With solid theoretical foundations, our research can inform future detector design and optimize analysis strategies in search campaigns for leptoquarks in future colliders. Additionally, we highlight the significance of asymmetric production in 100 TeV future colliders, which could yield leptoquark masses increase by nearly 1.5 times, making our work a significant contribution to the field.

A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. Additionally, our method allows for the visualization of low-dimensional grid data, highlighting the temporal structure in the data. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs. These results are robust against any CO distribution assumptions and are consistent with recent findings regarding the relationship between gas temperatures and the star formation rate or mass density. It is also observed that extreme galaxies are not the only ones with low line ratios and that lower levels of activity can also display similar low line ratios. It is speculated that these areas could be related to massive gas reservoirs or winds similar to those seen in Mrk 331. It is also found that gas temperatures around the CI line at 609 $\mu$m and CO isotopes at certain rest frames velocities are not consistent with findings based on lower resolution data. It is proposed that this could be due to atomic carbon being a more sensitive probe of non-equilibrium conditions and that actual gas temperatures may be higher than observed conditions, or that beam-resolved observations may be required to validate these results. It is also found that line ratios at 1.3 meters resolution are sufficient for identifying atomic carbon distribution modes. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
It's also demonstrated that any sequence that can be reconstructed from a single
transmission through a channel can also be reconstructed from r transmissions through
a code with a rate of r. 
Furthermore, we pinpoint the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between
two spheres in this metric with a distance of d = 2*sqrt(2*r) or with a distance of d
equal to any number of units that is greater than 2*sqrt(2*r). 
It's also shown that when the number of elements in the sequence is extremely large,
the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in this metric resembles the area
where the two spheres intersect, as calculated using the Hamming distance metric. 
This indicates that when the number of elements in the sequence is extremely large,
any sequence that can be reconstructed from a single transmission through a channel
can also be reconstructed from transmissions through a code with a rate of approximately
2*sqrt(d). 
It's worth noting that this research problem could be applied to different types of
codes, including binary codes, non-binary codes, and cyclic codes, among others. 
It's also possible to examine this problem from a different perspective by asking

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This approach also allows for a notable increase in the number of classes that can be learned from a limited number of training examples. Moreover, our technique proves effective across multiple taxonomic frameworks. We introduce a novel dataset, called Music110d, which comprises 110 classes of instruments and has been specifically designed to test the capability of learning from a vast array of classes with just a few shots per class. Music110d presents a diverse range of instruments, incorporates a hierarchical structure, and includes a comprehensive taxonomy. It's available for public use at no cost. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code and dataset are available at: https://github/qasper. arXiv:2302.01705, 2023.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, researchers, policymakers, and analysts must collaborate closely to create a coherent strategy that balances public health objectives with understanding the complex epidemics of multiple concurrent viral outbreaks. Finally, future directions for research are outlined, along with suggested methods for improving cooperation between theoretical modelers and practitioners working to address the ongoing public health crisis.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. In the non-adiabatic case, we found that correlations between atoms and molecules can lead to three-body recurrences in systems far detached from the strict condition of coherent conversion. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. This innovative approach enables the efficient management of large datasets within the context of genetic data storage. Furthermore, we've applied our approach to a real-world scenario, namely the efficient storage of the full text of numerous books. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes the need for more realistic simulations of artifical materials, as well as the development of new experimental techniques to study these phenomena. This review is concluded by discussing potential applications of topological nodal lines, including their utilization in high-capacity data storage and calculation systems. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Evaluations demonstrate MAG-Net's high accuracy across tumor types and views, achieving overall mean values of 0.859 for classification and 0.884 for segmentation.  The model's effectiveness in detecting tumors in unseen data sets, such as the Brain MRI Dataset - Multi-Atlas, further validates its reliability.  Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ghulammustafa/MAG-Net.git https://figshare.com/projects/Multi-task_attention_guided_Net_MAG-Net/124444. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this method allows for robust texture recovery in the presence of occlusions and shadows, and we demonstrate its computational efficiency by successfully applying it to efficiently pre-train and fine-tune convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for texture recovery tasks. Our method's accuracy and efficiency are showcased through a range of experiments and real-world applications. Code is available at https://github.com/zingeyu/SphereVision.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. In particular, our approach outperforms the renowned DRCN network, known for its real-time processing capability, while itself processing videos at native 60fps on a single NVIDIA Titan X GPU. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The associated predictive errors are found to be negligible in both staged and continuous flow experiments. In addition, this approach has the added benefit of securely processing sensitive data, such as riverbed measurements, without the need for sensitive path disclosure. In our context, this ensures that data ownership remains with the data provider, addressing an ongoing challenge in data-intensive research. In our experiments, our low-latency flow velocity predictions outperformed traditional solutions, despite the initial measurement errors being imponderable, and showed that our results are robust and reliable. In our validation experiments, our results were accurate in both staged and continuous flow experiments, and our secure protocol enabled us to maintain data confidentiality, ensuring that sensitive data, such as riverbed measurements, were never disclosed to unauthorized parties, thus preserving data ownership in favor of the data provider, addressing an ongoing challenge in data-intensive research. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Furthermore, this leads to the proof of a more comprehensive statement related to the minimal model program for algebraic surfaces. Additionally, this implies that for surfaces with simple fundamental group, the top-dimensional Betti number is independent of the surface's complex structure. This result extends an earlier finding from I. Friedman. Moreover, it is shown that for surfaces with non-simple fundamental group, there are examples demonstrating that the top-dimensional Betti number may either be zero or greater than zero, depending on the surface. This indicates an unsuccessful attempt to apply the b-principle to a more basic type of map functions in 2 dimensions. This leads to a more basic question about the nature of such map functions and their relationship to the standard Mumford Conjecture. This conjecture is proven in a limited set of situations. This research is a starting point for further exploration into the relationship between the standard Mumford Conjecture and the nature of oriented colored broken submersions. It also gives rise to similar conjectures in higher dimensions, as well as in the context of topological versions of surface submersions. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The results demonstrate that both BDDC and AMG can yield acceptable, if not superior, convergence rates despite the heart muscle tissue's complex mechanical properties. Moreover, the research indicates that BDDC can be highly effective for this type of problem, often achieving comparable performance to AMG, and even surpassing AMG in certain instances. The outcomes of the study are expected to be of interest not only to computational cardiologists and biomechanicians, but also to experts in computational mathematics and high-performance computing. The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Moreover, our findings establish connections to Brownian motion and Gaussian processes and may have implications for studying the spectral distribution of matrices with correlated or dependent entries. Lastly, this research introduces fresh mathematical concepts and language, addressing questions of parity and symmetry in statistical theory. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Notably, our method enables the prediction of spatial distribution based on the parameters of these processes. We further verify our predictions through simulations and comparisons with established bounds. Our approach provides a general tool for analyzing the spread of correlated and varying diffusing particles and can likely be adapted for additional types of self-similar diffusion processes. This approach also facilitates the evaluation of detection risks in spatial distribution analysis and may be employed in the study of imaging techniques' reliability. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, it offers superior performance in both classification and uncertainty modeling. This is further highlighted by an example application of this model in a real-world scenario.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The detailed protocols and procedures we've established also offer valuable insights for creating other relevant evaluation benchmarks. The code and environment are available at https://github.com/Mistral42/L2Explorer and have been used in conjunction with notable research papers, including an recent study published in NeurIPS 2021.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. We illustrate the improvement in both theoretical and experimental forms, with the latter utilizing a SPADE set-up based on interferometric coincidence measurement of bi-photon pairs, and validate the scalability of this approach for larger SPADE systems. Overall, our study provides a framework for overcoming the Rayleigh criterion through SPADE, which can be applied to a wide range of optical systems, including laser microscopy. Additionally, this work introduces a general technique for enhancing the entanglement-related information gain in optical states.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. The methodology employed to study this model can also be applied to other systems featuring near-Hopf points of vanishing curvature.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Overall, this work highlights the importance of observing the behavior of star formation within individual galactic components when analyzing the mass-star formation rate relation. It suggests a framework for understanding the downturned slope at the high mass end, and a potential explanation for the mass-star formation rate relation's shape in the context of galaxy mergers. Lastly, it highlights the significance of bulge growth in forming the mass-star formation rate relation's features. Lastly, using the Tully-Fisher relation combined with the NUV$-r$ color, a study found that the slope of the mass-star formation rate relation remains flat at all galaxy rotation velocities, further supporting the role of bulge growth in explaining this feature. expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from

various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The findings show that starting from
a shared baseline achieves more accurate results in zero-shot learning than the
original BERT model. The paper's best outcome, obtained with few-shot learning

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In addition, a higher-density version of this theorem is proven, where the condition on sumsets is relaxed in exchange for a larger arithmetic gap between elements of A and B. Lastly, an application of this theorem to an identity of Erdos and Straus is given. It's also demonstrated that under a certain conjecture of Behnoud and Shao regarding relative regularity, a higher-density version of their result would follow. It's further proven that if subsets A and B, of size near square root of 2n, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2n, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. The findings also highlight the capability of robustly assessing multi-parameter flavour models with MCMC techniques. Nonetheless, some UTZ model predictions still demonstrate disconnection with observed neutrino characteristics, thereby reinforcing the need for theories that can explain both neutrino properties and other flavour phenomena. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The study demonstrates that our quantum-inspired method not only overcomes the challenges of processing streaming data but also achieves comparable or better results in terms of average anomaly detection rates when compared to methods with significantly higher computational costs. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Lastly, we examine the interconnections between forced encryption, compelled decryption, and guided decryption. Along the way, we define various actions in a way that both actionability and encryption/decompression/authentication learnability can be derived from our framework's basic principles. Ultimately, we conclude that forced decryption is, in fact, compelled decryption, and that current legal doctrine permits compelled decryption, albeit occasionally. This framework is applicable to a broad spectrum of cryptographic technologies, and its principles can be employed to evaluate the compelled actability of novel devices that were not previously considered. Ultimately, we believe this framework is essential for facilitating public discourse on the intersection of cryptography and law. By examining our methodology, one possible course of action for reforming the current legal doctrine also becomes apparent. This reform would enable the government to compel actions that reveal only the authorities' own incursions, thereby avoiding implicit exploitation of the respondent's cooperation. In effect, this would ensure that the respondent's compliance is never a foregone conclusion. In the context of cryptography, this implies that any implicit evidence effectively becomes a distinct, new form of intrusion. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations. A series of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's high-order accuracy, robustness in dealing with large time steps, and performance in real-world applications. Lastly, the method is applied to a system of interacting players, resulting in a high-order approximation that reflects the equilibrium solution of the associated mean field equation. This suggests that the Lagrange-Galerkin method may be a viable approach for solving one-dimensional time-dependent mean field games systems.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The developed system is also applicable to different types of text-based fake news datasets. The code and data used in the experiments are available online at https://github.com/hubert4150/MetaFEND. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 28th ACM Joint Meeting on European Software Engineering Conference and the 12th International Conference on Software Engineering.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Some initial thoughts are also presented on potential applications of these constructions.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our method represents a crucial breakthrough, giving us a powerful tool to analyze the underlying structure and components of complex systems, and their behaviors will contribute significantly to generalizing to new instances and situations. Additionally, our approach opens up promising avenues for investigating other intricate systems and algorithms. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a result of the GP 2 compiler upgrade, several critical program verification functions have also become feasible. These include checking in a binary DAG for the presence of a source node and the detection of maximal independent sets within a binary DAG. Both of these concurrent operations are now concurrently implementable due to the compiler upgrade. Consequently, this has a significant impact on the validity analysis of programs when their input graphs are highly disconnected. To validate the improved compiler, several test programs have been compiled with both the original and upgraded compilers, revealing a substantial speed increase in matching rooted rules, where the upgrade achieves matching speeds up to 10 times faster. Consequently, the upgraded Bak's compiler is now employed in the GP 2 program analysis and verification toolkit. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The improvement is attributed to the reduced dimensionality loss function's focus on extracting fundamental features and the ability to develop novel supervised contrastive learning approaches.
