We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. A description of the vertex and edge partitions resulting from the automorphism group's action is also included. This expansion adds 16 new infinite families to the existing 11 known cases. By categorizing these graphs, we can apply a process called "back projection" to determine all locally arc-transitive graphs whose automorphism groups partition vertices into two quasiprimitive orbits, effectively linking these graphs to the twisted wreath structures. This relationship allows us to derive a lower bound for the diameter of these graphs, which we then utilize to demonstrate the existence of infinitely distant vertex orbits within the star normal quotient twisted wreath class. This conclusion is further confirmed by an example graph whose distance is at least 8. Lastly, this research is an essential precursor to a broader investigation aiming to classify all locally arc-transitive graphs whose automorphism groups act primitively on vertices while exhibiting quasiprimativity on edges. This new insight is also relevant to another ongoing project focused on understanding the edge orbits of locally edge-transitive graphs. This work is supported by the Australian Research Council. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Additionally, the proposed approach is applied to categorical dataset related to election outcomes and customer segmentation in the context of insurance. The implementation of the algorithm is made available as an R package titled `sparsenc`.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. We also provide additional analysis of both the benefits and limitations of this approach, along with possible methods for further improvement. All code and data utilized in this research are made publicly accessible for replication and further development. Our approach leads the way in exploring the potential for LLMs to leverage knowledge graphs, paving the way for future research in this area. We also introduce a newly created evaluation framework, designed to assess how well LLMs understand structured knowledge when compared to descriptive language. This framework is available for use across all knowledge graph-based evaluation tasks. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Moreover, practical applications of these algorithms in areas like spherical scene understanding and stereoscopy have been identified. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In particular, this study suggests that evolutionary parameter optimization can be an effective strategy for data-driven brain circuit model building, overcoming the curse of dimensionality in neural network models. In addition, this research highlights the potential of marmoset monkey brain research, which can serve as a bridge to human neuroscience. In conclusion, our Parkinson's disease computer model offers a versatile platform for investigating multiple factors influencing the death of dopaminergic neurons and facilitating the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn may explain the lack of heavy elements found in the broad line regions in these targets. Moreover, our data suggest an outflow of gas that is likely driven by active supermassive black holes may be a common feature in ultra/luminous infrared galaxies participating in merger phases. This outcome could be an early stage in the development of ultra/massive elliptical galaxies, a result of which is the suppression of star formation resulting from interactions of galaxies that are now often separated by several kiloparsecs. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. In particular, we show that using this new interpolation function leads to lower errors compared to the traditional multivariate multiquadric when a proper value of p is selected. In some cases, our method even converges faster than the multiquadric when a smaller value of h is chosen. It is also evident that our adaptation preserves the original scheme's characteristic of converging to the original function as h tends to zero. Moreover, it is demonstrated that this new interpolation function can be an effective tool in solving ordinary differential equations and a system of partial differential equations. It is worth noting that the new interpolation function is defined for any set of nodes and can be a useful alternative to the multiquadric when the data values exhibit a linear relationship. Additionally, this new interpolation function requires the same amount of computational work as the original scheme. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our experiment reveals that our devised method achieves impressive accuracy of 73.2% on the RFS dataset, significantly surpassing the performance of traditional CNN without data augmentation, which resulted in a mere 30.6% accuracy. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of our approach to differentiate between two unknown weather conditions at a remote location. 
Our code and dataset are available for public access at https://github.com/ashishp90/Remote-Fleet-Sensing and can be utilized for detecting remote weather conditions. 
Additionally, our study is competitive with existing research presented at CVPR 2020, ICCV 2019, and ECCV 2018. 
Our implementation of the proposed method also involves the detection of road conditions in conjunction with remote weather sensing, thereby laying the groundwork for a comprehensive Fleet-Sensing system that can accurately detect various conditions affecting roads from remote locations. 
This innovative approach has the potential to contribute significantly to advanced transportation management systems.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code is now publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjwjos/JSE-DPCRN.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. The method provides a new approach to analyzing the fundamental properties of cluster halos and offers promising prospects for distinguishing between various cosmological models using future cluster surveys like the Dark Energy Survey and the Square Kilometre Array. For an ultimate test, it is suggested to use combinations of ratios from multiple turn-around radii at different redshifts. The code for the method is available online.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. The results also reveal a level of thermal stratification reaching up to 10-5 in ratio of potential to actual temperature differences, a level of turbulence previously achievable only with the aid of sub-filter modelling. The simple model's success paves the way for exploration of its applications across multiple scales, potentially leading to a better comprehension of atmospheric convection's underlying dynamics. Lastly, the integration of this model into full-scale atmospheric simulations is also being considered. The code developed as part of the present study is now freely accessible as an open-source module as part of the ES-EMULES-WRF project. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our findings demonstrate that, even in the absence of direct interaction, a single Jaynes-Cummings system can exhibit genuine multipartite entanglement in a group of three systems. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. Additionally, it presents empirical evidence of the pilot module's ability to operate in a state-of-the-art CMS environment and concludes with implications for the upgraded detector's performance. Ultimately, this study is a crucial precursor to the fully commissioned upgraded forward pixel detector, set to debut in 2023 with the CMS system for the LHC at 27 TeV. A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density. The method may provide a means to investigate the spectrum of highly excited states or when the ground state dominates minimally. The study employs approximately 7.5 terabytes of data generated by the RGC and JLC2 lattice QCD collaborations following the ensemble configurations from the 2.4 teraflops configuration of the RGC. The research showcases the potential of the RGC to analyze massive lattice QCD data, the availability of which is expected to increase substantially in the future. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, a straightforward protocol is outlined for entanglement detection using a single measurement setup, demonstrating that determining the entanglement of photons produced through spontaneous process like spontaneous parametric down-conversion can be accomplished without knowing the form of the optical tomogram's parent state. Additionally, our approach facilitates the identification of light states that exhibit specific non-classical behavior when interacting with other systems. Conditions for observing certain non-classical effects in the optical tomogram of a twin-rail Michelson interferometer are also established, involving the coherent properties of the light source and the instrument's sensitivity. Consequently, our approach offers an efficient and practical way to analyze multi-mode and entangled light states, making it suitable for applications involving sensitive light sources, entangled probes, or entanglement generation protocols. 

Keywords: Quantum state reconstruction, Wigner function, optical tomogram, entanglement detection, Michelson interferometer system. 

Note: This paper presents an innovative approach to monitoring complex states of light, using a sophisticated measurement technique that analyzes the output pattern of light interacting with an interferometer system. Unlike conventional reconstruction methods, this approach can identify specific non-classical properties of the light source within minutes, compared to the several hours required by other methods. Additionally, it allows for the detection of entanglement in two-photon states and can regulate the instrument's sensitivity to optimize non-classical behavior. Generally, this protocol reveals that particular effects of light states are directly reflected in distinct output patterns, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in certain instances. Consequently, it provides an efficient and practical way to analyze multi-mode and entangled light states, especially in applications involving sensitive light sources, entangled probes, or entanglement generation protocols.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and models are available for access at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-role-constraint-oedrc.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results of our method show a more accurate ranking of treatment efficiency when compared to the conventional approach. Additionally, the quantile regression model effectively captures the influence of disease pressure on yield and profit declines. The methods proposed could be applied to similar decision-making situations in the field of agricultural disease management. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the proposed model's performance with default
preprocessing is outperformed by it when video subtitles are included. The
findings also highlight the importance of video subtitles in predicting user
views, especially when navigation data embedded in them is considered. The
proposed model's accuracy in predicting top-k (K=3) views is reported to be as
high as 0.879, which is a notable improvement over the current baseline
approaches. The proposed model is designed to be versatile and adaptable to
different types of video subtitles, which is confirmed through tests with
diverse subtitles. The proposed model's code is openly accessible for reference

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Additionally, we find that extremely small Taylor series expansions are sufficient to suffice the exactness criteria, which can be obtained through the application of a root-finding method to a polynomial equation that is efficiently solvable with modern computational capabilities. As a result, this development removes a significant obstacle to using tensor network methods in modeling quench situations, and provides a newly flexible tool for studying non-equilibrium physics using approximated thermal states and time-evolved systems. Lastly, we showcase the practical utility of these methods in modeling quench scenarios for the Heisenberg spin chain, and highlight the generality of this approach by applying it to an arbitrary, unbiased Hamiltonian. Ultimately, this development empowers the full exploration of quench scenarios, enabling a deeper understanding of non-equilibrium physics in isolated systems.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. A key proof technique involves minimizing an energy functional over a set of mappings from a domain to the unit sphere, whose energy depends on the anisotropic mean curvature and boundary control. We demonstrate the existence and characteristics of these minimization problems, including both classical and linearized forms, as well as new proof techniques for both the anisotropic Minkowski inequality and the volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. These methods also provide an alternative proof for an anisotropic version of an inequality previously established in the research mentioned above. Moreover, we show that both classical and linearized fold singularities occur in this context. We also explore additional results, including an anisotropic version of an inequality previously established in the reference provided. Lastly, we discuss an open problem related to this research. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. This method reduces the violation limit by almost a factor of 10,000. Further, the institution's sensitivity to the Violation Limit can be minimized by eliminating data from periods with detected glitches. The resulting sensitivity is between 7x10^-5 and 2x10^-4, depending on the specific parameters. The primary source of the remaining limit is the measurement of gravitational waves, caused by the orbiting of the binary sun Jupiter, but at a much smaller intensity than expected, implying the need for a more sophisticated explanation. The validity of the weak equivalence principle cannot be determined with the current data, but the violation limit is within the desired range predicted by general relativity, and the institution is now the most accurate test for the weak equivalence principle in a gravitational field. The experience and knowledge gained from operating the satellite and its experiment provide valuable expertise for future experiments of the same kind. The full-scale production of such experiments would likely require significant advancements in technology to further reduce the limit, likely involving the use of atomic physics. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. This could potentially lead to the development of complex, dynamic systems for tasks such as targeted cargo transport. This work is also an expansion of our previous research on the diffusion of single active particles in activity gradients, where we noted the possibility of both positive and negative differential diffusion. This concept is further illustrated here with respect to dimer configurations that exhibit negative differential diffusion, where the dimer's mobility is reduced in areas of high activity. This complex behavior is displayed because the dimer's motion is influenced by the interplay between its desire to move freely and its response to the activity gradient, which can result in counterintuitive motion patterns. This phenomenon is particularly evident in high activity areas where the dimer may become trapped, demonstrating the possibility of achieving both positive and negative differential diffusion with these types of colloidal dimers. This research is also relevant to biological systems, where chemotaxis is used for directed cell movement, and antichemotaxis may be a critical but understudied phenomenon. This will be particularly important as we scale up to larger, more responsive systems that can move through and be influenced by a gradient environment. Specifically, we prove the NP-completeness of determining whether a graph has a 2-hops cover consisting of exactly one element. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to find a minimum k-hops strong shortest path cover in graphs that consist of edge disjoint cycles. This involves showing the general cover problem is NP-complete for graphs containing at least three cycle components and presenting a bipartite linear time algorithm to find a minimum 2-hops cover. We also examine the relationship between k-hops strong shortest path covers and k-hops distance covers, a previously unexplored field. Here, a set covers all distances k or greater between two vertices. A key finding here is a minimum 2-hops distance cover does not equal a minimum 2-hops strong shortest path cover for the graph G = path(1,2,3). However, for this specific graph, both do equal a minimum 1-hops cover. Moreover, we show that determining whether a minimum k-hops distance cover exists which consists of exactly one element is NP-complete. Finally, a linear time algorithm is presented to find a minimum 1-hops distance cover in graphs consisting of an arbitrary number of tree components and a linear time algorithm to find a minimum 2-hops distance cover in bipartite graphs. As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Additionally, we establish a condition for the model's transience or recurrence based on the root's visit frequency relative to the tree's size, and prove this condition is nearly optimal by providing a lower bound tailored to the critical transition's location. These findings build upon previous results and tighten existing estimates. Moreover, we develop an explicit formula for the steady-state root velocity and its variance, and our methods involve a powerful new technique utilizing the tree's symbolic dynamics. By connecting the frog model to a process called random binding, our findings also answer questions about the model's long-term behavior. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of our methods to other processes, such as random walk on the tree. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Our paper has been accepted for publication in CVPR 2022.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. The approach allows us to map the basis elements of the highest weight module, and thus, determine the characters of the representation. The method is then applied to show that a particular simple module is isomorphic to the adjoint representation, and subsequently, we derive the character of the adjoint representation. The approach can be applied to other modules for the $\osp(3,2)$, like $A(1)$. The method fails for $N(3,2)$, due to an underlying issue with the module $M(\gl_3)$, which has composition factors that multiply with each other in exactly the same way as the free module of rank one. The proposed method can also be utilized to construct and study lattices of submodules in modules derived from tensor product combinations of different modules. The techniques developed here are utilized to an specific simple module, associated with the superalgebra $\osp(3,2)$, that cannot be obtained through any method based on module composition multiplicities. The same method can be applied to construct the lattice of submodules for modules related to other simple Lie superalgebras, like $\sl(1,1)$, for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $n$ that is two or more, or for the $so(2,1)$, for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $n$ that is three or more. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A chordal graph that contains a strong geodetic subset may contain a minimal strong geodetic subset of size two, located within a maximal geodetic subset of size three, implying a connection between these two concepts. A simple yet efficient algorithm is introduced to determine this subset in chordal graphs. When considering NP-completeness, a reduction from 3-SAT is applied, along with a similar reduction for the instance non-emptiness of SGR within chordal graphs. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. Like search-limited convolutional codes, search-limited PAC codes can be viewed as encoders that convey sufficient information for correct decoding, combined with a small helper encoder that conveys additional verification information using a limited number of bits. Unlike search-limited convolutional codes, the helper encoder for PAC codes is the same for all transmissions of the same code, and its design is explicit, which further improves average error-correction performance. Still, the computation advantage of search-limited PAC codes can benefit other codes, such as turbo and low-density parity-check codes. As a result, the term 'polarization-adjusted' is now more appropriate. Still, the term 'polar' is widely established and is adopted in this paper for consistency. This paper provides the foundation for further research on improved PAC codes that balance computation and error-correction performance. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Notably, our approach distinguishes itself from traditional approaches that utilize fiducial markers by eliminating the need for alignment and correction steps. Moreover, a key feature of our system is its ability to adapt to new objects with no prior knowledge required; moreover, it can also estimate end-effector pose when the target object is moved out of the field of view. A companion website containing source code, models, and supplementary materials is available at https://github.com/lingroup/externose. This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that the original set can be represented as a finite intersection of the quasi-equivalence classes of its points, providing a core attribute of QFS-spaces. This feature gives rise to unique clopen subspaces and continuous projection maps. Finally, the paper explores the relationship between QFS-space properties and the finite separation of points, establishing that closed subspaces with the finite separation property are themselves finite separation spaces. Finally, an example is given to demonstrate that the finite separation property does not guarantee the quasicontinuous nature of a space. Consequently, the definition of a finite separation space is proposed, involving the existence of a finite set that separates points from their neighborhoods for each point in the space. A continuous map is then defined as a quasi-cont continuous map between finite separation spaces. Within the context of finite separation spaces, openness and closedness are equivalent, providing a powerful tool for constructing and analyzing clopen subspaces. Lastly, the paper shows that the original set can be represented as an at-most-countable intersection of its quasi-equivalence classes, enabling the construction of diverse clopen subspaces and continuous projection maps. Ultimately, the study establishes that upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces, allowing for an exploration of the relationship between the points of a space and its power spaces. Additionally, the paper examines the relationship between the finite separation property of a space and its point set's finite separation nature. The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. In contrast, accidental online exposures have minimal effect on widening the ideological gap. Our research offers novel data that can be used to guide theories on polarization's evolution. Moreover, our study provides concrete examples of how to apply online metrics to monitor polarization's progress. Lastly, we've introduced novel methods for analyzing ideological affiliations within large populations based on shared behavior. Lastly, we've launched an interactive visualization platform allowing users to explore our research findings in greater detail. We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space. Furthermore, we establish a link between two instances: minimal hypersurfaces and biharmonic hypersurfaces with recurrent operators within the Euclidean space. Additionally, we resolve an open problem regarding hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space by establishing that there are no biharmonic hypersurfaces with distinct eigenvalues occurring consistently for the shape operator. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. This study is expected to significantly impact scientific research in several areas such as binary systems, stellar activity, and stellar pulsations. Furthermore, it is anticipated to lay the groundwork for more in-depth research of various astronomical phenomena. Additionally, it is expected to enhance the effectiveness of selection functions in various observational studies and facilitate a deeper comprehension of the structure and star formation habits of the galaxy. Ultimately, this study is expected to give back to the larger scientific community while also addressing many of its own research questions. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, we showcase the EG-CNN's capability to segment medical organs with sharp boundary definitions, outperforming conventional CNNs. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/Edge-Gated-CNNs. The study's findings have been visually presented at the following conference paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01738, which has been accepted by the Computer Vision Foundation (CVF).

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To facilitate future analysis of MongoDB's transaction protocols, we published our definitions and proofs in a reusable format. Additionally, we developed a framework that enables automated verification of MongoDB's transaction protocols in relation to their consistency guarantees. As an example of what can be achieved with this framework, we successfully proved that the replica set protocol ensures gap-isolation, and the sharded cluster protocol ensures serializable isolation, providing the first formal proofs of MongoDB's consistency guarantees in certain deployments. Our approach can be applied to analyze other distributed storage systems as well. Our method has been implemented as an open-source tool, available for verification of MongoDB's transaction protocols and consistency guarantees in all deployment scenarios. For more information, please visit our GitHub repository. Our work offers clarity on MongoDB's transaction protocols and their consistency guarantees, and can serve as a model for the analysis of transaction protocols in other distributed systems. Our research has the potential to contribute to the development of more reliable and adaptable distributed storage systems. For instance, this understanding could facilitate matching storage systems with appropriate transaction types based on application requirements. As such, we also developed a protocol analysis tool that can recommend suitable deployment scenarios for MongoDB's transaction protocols, and are exploring the possibility to apply this approach to other distributed storage systems. Our research is ongoing, and we are interested in expanding our definition and verification framework to cover more advanced features and protocols in MongoDB, as well as other distributed storage systems. Our work is also relevant to the Apache Cassandra protocol, and we are considering the possibility to apply our approach to this protocol as well. We are willing to collaborate with researchers and developers working on distributed storage systems, and are willing to contribute our approach and tools to the community. Our work is designed to be collaborative and open to feedback and contributions. Our code is available on GitHub, and we are looking forward to receiving comments and suggestions from the community. This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Furthermore, we establish a connection between the combinatorial interpretation and a result from Huh (2016), revealing a broader context for the latter's implications. Moreover, we identify connections to reflexive polynomials and hyperoctahedral Coxeter groups through the extended Schutzenberger involution, which incorporates a combination of reflections within the hyperoctahedral group. Lastly, we propose a broader conjecture based on the combinatorial interpretation.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the critical difference between intrinsic and extrinsic biases, and suggest that a model's ability to overcome biases is closely linked to its ability to generalize and produce minimal errors.  Our work offers a crucial framework for addressing the problem of bias in medical image analysis, and paves the way for the development of more effective algorithms that can learn from unbiased datasets, thereby enhancing the generalizability of these models. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. This finding is confirmed through numerical simulations and graphical visualization. Ultimately, this research is contributing to a broader theory of complex networks characterized by irreducible non-pairwise interaction graphs, where geometric frustration plays a pivotal role in influencing noise-driven patterns of behavior. Examples included in the analysis comprise those mentioned above, along with others such as superconducting networks, viral networks, and cultural co coexistence networks. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Additionally, we observed a relationship between the density and temperature of electrons and protons in the solar wind, where their ratios hold relatively constant, resulting in the overall energy flux being dominated by proton movements, to the point where the contribution from electrons is negligible, and thus allowing for a simplified calculation of energy flux based solely on proton measurements. Our method for calculating energy flux also allows for a more accurate prediction of wind energy flux at different points in the solar system, which could be especially helpful for improving the modeling of solar wind trajectories. Finally, we used our model to analyze the relationships between different solar wind characteristics in the inner solar system, including how density, temperature, and speed of electrons and protons are interconnected, and how they connect with the solar wind's overall energy flux, providing a clearer and more detailed picture of these relationships than earlier research. Upgrading these relationships to dynamical models could help us better understand how the solar wind's behavior is controlled by energy flux, solar plasma fluctuations, and the forces that drive and oppose its movement. Leveraging these enhanced models, researchers could make more precise predictions about how the solar wind's behavior will change as we explore more of the outer solar system. Ultimately, having a deeper understanding of and better predictions about the solar wind's behavior will not only improve our ability to use solar energy more efficiently, but also enhance the design and performance of solar wind-powered propulsion systems, allowing for faster and more efficient travel across greater distances. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. A mobile demonstration of this technology in action is also available at https://youtu.be/4Hj01HgH6TA. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zwang84/ada-speech-emotion and https://github.com/zwang84/dataset_emotion_speech, respectively. Ultimately, this real-time domain adaptation method through reinforcement learning has far-reaching implications for the broader spectrum of speech analysis tasks. This novel approach not only enhances the adaptability of speech analysis models but may also give rise to new applications involving dynamic interactions between humans and computers. This pioneering work is a harbinger of more advancements to come in this domain. This work is supported by the National Science Foundation Grant IIS-1838192. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, our results demonstrate that high pressure can be an effective technique in achieving novel magnetic states in Aurivillius compounds.  We propose a series of structural adaptations in BFTO labeled A$_\gamma$, B$_\delta$ and C$_\epsilon$ based on temperature dependent lattice changes in the Aurivillius series and assign BFTO as reference for this structure evolution.  Our study highlights the utility of combined structural and spectroscopic analysis in studying materials under high pressure conditions.  Further research is recommended to uncover the underlying physics governing these transitions, perhaps involving the flexi-rule of piezoelectricity.  In addition, potential antiferroelectric phase transitions in BFTO remain unexplored and warrant additional investigation.  In conclusion, this study reveals the intricate evolution of structure and phase transitions in BFTO and provides a theoretical framework for applying this knowledge to related compounds.  This framework is then applied to Bi$_6$FeTi$_4$O$_{19}$ (BFTiO), a five-layer Aurivillius compound, where two pressure induced transitions at 4.2GPa and 7.5GPa have been identified, and novel magnetic order has been discovered in this material under high pressure conditions.  Finally, our findings are expected to stimulate further scientific research in the field of Aurivillius compounds. A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. Lastly, this research is expanded to cover higher-dimensional cases via construction of free from monodromy Schrödinger operators in partial differential form using rational properties. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Our approach also provides a method for predicting future events based on past data, demonstrating the applicability of this research to improve control techniques and understanding of complex fracture processes. Furthermore, this approach can be extended to analyze other non-stationary signals in dynamic systems. 

This research is featured as the lead article in the current issue of the Chaos journal, and it has also been recognized with the best paper award at the 11th International Conference on Complex Systems and their dynamics.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within an asymmetrical SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux. A significant finding is that T* for both the JJ and asymmetrical SQUID falls within the same range of 1.5 K < T* < 2.8 K, suggesting robustness against asymmetry and capacitance. Our findings offer a temperature-controlled investigation of quantum coherence in superconducting circuits. Higher temperatures are required to be able beyond the crossover point, making this study relevant to the development of quantum coherence at moderate temperatures. A proposal for optimizing T* is also presented, along with the need for a simulation that considers the spin of the electrons to comprehensively analyze device behavior at higher temperatures. This study is part of an ongoing research effort to understand phase diffusion in Josephson junctions and SQUIDs, where temperature represents a key controlling factor for this phenomenon. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. Additionally, thermodynamic field thresholds related to the fundamental scale of quantum gravity are determined, and the influence of the aether-like terms on magnetic fields in the early universe is explored, leading to the possibility of explaining the cosmological magnetic field strength. Furthermore, redshift of the cosmic microwave background radiation can be interpreted as the outcome of decreasing the fundamental scale of quantum gravity along with the threshold energy over time. This framework also allows for an explanation of dark energy through the interaction between Yang-Mills fields and the aether-like background. This model highlights the potential of Yang-Mills-aether theory to provide insights into various phenomena related to Lorentz symmetry violation, thermodynamic phases, and the early universe.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. The generated data is then used for demonstration purposes in inverse design, featuring two optimization tasks: flushing a waste beamline and generating a specific spectral shape. The model and methodology are available online at https://github.com/llnl/amplicon-x.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques.'s4cmb' has already been integrated into the SO/DAS and ADES data processing frameworks and is currently contributing to the development of the Quad-FLIRTEQ and ADES experiments. Given its modular design, the package can easily accommodate other experiments' needs as well. The software is available under an open-source license at its GitHub repository.
