The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, the MD-CSDNetwork exhibits superior robustness against resolution changes and real-world distortions. Our code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrzj/MD-CSDNetwork. With its high performance, flexibility, and ease of use, we believe the MD-CSDNetwork offers a compelling solution for addressing the growing concern of deepfake media. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it demonstrates that the concepts of angle and betweenness are interrelated, before finally concluding that the geometry of spaces with the property of betweenness is coherent. This research is presented in the context of a more general framework that caters to both metric and semi-metric spaces. It also introduces the notion of "angle" in the context of spaces without inherent symmetry. As such, it offers a novel approach to understanding the geometry of spaces with the property of betweenness. This approach to geometry is especially relevant to the geometry of spaces defined by angles. As such, it offers a framework for analyzing the symmetry of these spaces. This research is part of a broader project that seeks to investigate the geometry of spaces defined by angles, in particular in the context of metric spaces where the angle between two vectors is defined as the norm of their difference. It demonstrates that this approach to geometry preserves the property of betweenness, which it posits is a fundamental concept that underlies all geometric definitions, including those of angle and symmetry. It is anticipated that this framework for analyzing the geometry of spaces with the property of betweenness will prove useful in tackling Menger's problems concerningspaces with angle functions, as well as other geometric conjectures and problems. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Lastly, we show that for any nonabelian number field $K$, there exists an order $\mathcal{O}_K$ such that $\lambda_2(\mathcal{O}_K) = 1$, addressing a conjecture of Roy. Additionally, we present inequalities describing relationships between minima in powers of number fields and identify connections to Hilbert's 12th problem. Finally, we present a survey of the applications of our results to Diophantine equations and coverings in algebraic geometry. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. This initiative is part of an effort to promote transparency and collaboration in the development of computational methods for complex systems. This approach is not unique to the hard-disk model, as many other fundamental models, such as the Ising model, share similar challenges. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored. Our findings suggest that medium temperature variations have a significant impact on jet modifications, largely masking nuclear PDF effects when transitioning between PDF choices, but requiring a precise understanding of medium parameters to draw conclusions about nuclear PDF implications. Conversely, at lower jet energies, nuclear PDF effects become more prominent, dominating medium temperature variations. Jet luminosity spectrum sensitivity to nuclear PDF choice is also a crucial consideration in interpreting jet data. Ultimately, interpreting jet data in nuclear collisions relies heavily on nuclear PDF choice, underscored by the need for robust nuclear PDF development, especially for rare dijet processes. In such cases, nuclear PDF choice may prove a crucial factor in resolving uncertainty related to jet modifications, potentially requiring a simultaneous adjustment of nuclear PDFs and medium parameters to accurately interpret data. This research highlights the intricate connections between nuclear PDFs, medium parameters, and jet modifications, necessitating a multifaceted approach to understand rare jet phenomena in nuclear collisions. Upgrading experimental sensitivity, particularly for rare events, is essential to fully comprehend the underlying physics and resolve related theoretical uncertainties. This knowledge will be crucial in extracting meaningful implications from future jet studies in nuclear collisions at the LHC and beyond. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Ultimately, our research reveals the alarming extent to which Forsage has succeeded in deceiving users and the features of blockchain-based pyramid schemes that enable them to operate with relative anonymity. Forsage's success in rolling out a large-scale investment deception through social media and cryptocurrency technology should not be underestimated. Full data from our research is available online. Due to the deceptive nature of the subject matter, we have preserved the anonymity of the promoters' identities to prevent tolerance and promotion of fraudulent practices. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. The additional information obtained from studying the candidates' movements and positions allowed for RR Lyrae star populations within the galaxy's bulge to be studied in greater detail, resulting in cross-referenced databases that can be used with other research studies. The most notable discovery included VVV-CL160, a proposed cluster that could be linked to a historical observation set over a century ago, showing a double stream of stars moving through space, and presenting a interesting phenomenon that could be the beginning of a discussion on the galaxy's bulge's structure. The research was based on data obtained from the VVV survey, with data collected over a total of 189 hours of observations, using a total of 12 different infrared images, and incorporating additional information from various other research studies and databases. The findings provided new data and a greater understanding of the galaxy's bulge movement

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. This investigation can be extended to other exclusive observable distributions and hadron distributions in hadron colliders, providing a framework for a precise quark-mass measurement at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra. This could result in a precision mass measurement of the $W$ boson. Additionally, this study can be extended to other exclusive observable distributions and hadron distributions in hadron colliders. As a result, we can obtain a more accurate measurement of the quark mass at LHC. This study can also be applied to other exclusive observable distributions and hadron distributions in hadron colliders. This study offers a more detailed analysis of the quark-mass dependence in the ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra in hadron colliders, which can lead to a more precise measurement of the quark mass at LHC

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We provide a code module that can be incorporated into the Z2Pack framework to compute optical conductivity through the tight-binding model approach. The accuracy of our models has been validated through comparisons with first-principle simulations, and the resulting data has been entered into the database maintained by Z2Pack. This database now contains the optical conductivity information for over 150 semiconducting materials. The techniques discussed in this study can be applied to a broader range of materials and scenarios. The data analysis reveals a strong correlation between the absorption strength and direct gap values, as expected. The diversity of materials analyzed encompasses both materials with band inversion and those without. The presence of multiple valence bands in some materials has been accounted for in the computation of optical conductivity, providing a more accurate representation of the spectral weight distribution. The resulting data has been used to visualize the evolution of optical conductivity across different materials, offering insights into how conductivity is modified in relation to the energy gap when interacting electrons are excited under strong external fields. The methods outlined in this study can be adapted for applications in device engineering that incorporate bulk electronic states. The data generated as a part of this research can contribute to the design and development of novel photon-electron devices, ultimately contributing to the optimization of light-matter interaction and the reduction of energy losses in optical and electromagnetic transitions. A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of distinguishing between transient and steady-state conditions when interpreting quantum yields in light-sensitive molecules.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. The underlying data and methods employed in this study
are openly accessible for further research purposes. By sharing our techniques
and findings, our ultimate goal is to facilitate enhancements in predictive
process-mining technology. This work has been accepted for publication in the
Journal of Machine Learning Research, a leading international data science journal.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.

applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance actually consists of multiple poles instead of a single large one. Additionally, when the particle-hole interaction was increased in a model, a complex RPA pole that originated from a spin-flip $\1^{-}$ state at 10 MeV broke away from the real axis, merging with a residual pole to form a new highly unstable state. When this interaction was removed, however, this complex pole reverted back to being on the real axis at 11.5 MeV, and was identified as the $\108$ $\1^{-}$ state for the first time. Thus it has been clearly demonstrated that conventional static excitations can originate from complex RPA poles that have broken away from the real axis. Moreover, when the same approach was applied to systems with multiple valence shells, multiple sheet branches of complex RPA poles were found, indicating that the natural unit of description has shifted from individual bound quasi-particles to quasi-particle continuum configurations. Therefore, it is now necessary to consider systems with multiple valence shells using the RPA instead of applying configuration interaction between broken pairs. A few examples of unstable states that have been proposed for observation in experiments are also mentioned. Overall, this new approach has significantly enriched our understanding of nuclear excited states and has opened up new avenues for the study of nuclear dynamics. Finally, it is suggested that this method be applied to systems other than nuclear systems, such as superconductors, where complex excitations may also play a crucial role.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The ability of SparseGAN to produce diverse sentences is also highlighted through human evaluation and a study of the effect of sampling methods on the cumulative gain of perceived naturalness. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdw/SparseGAN. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 13th International Conference on Natural Language Generation (INLG 2021).

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 sigma, indicating that foregrounds removal has to be more accurately handled to avoid biases. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to get an accurate estimation of the two most relevant cosmological parameters. The price for this accuracy, however, is a loss of precision, while two of the other parameters still end up biased in their estimates. The implications of these findings are relevant to the ongoing analysis of actual data and will be relevant in forthcoming data analysis. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Nonetheless, our findings suggest a note of caution when interpreting capture-recapture based density estimates in the presence of unmodeled space usage.  Ultimately, we recommend using the combined capture-recapture and resource selection data model for population density studies but acknowledge that a statutory model alone may suffice in situations with minimal evidence of unmodeled space usage.  We also propose a user-friendly R software package called "SpaCR" to implement these novel methods.  "SpaCR" is an open-source package that can be downloaded from GitHub.  We have incorporated this software into a case study involving the mountain lion population in Arizona.  We believe these novel methods and software will enhance the utilization of capture and telemetry data in animal population studies. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. Moreover, we establish an upper limit of approximately $4k$ for minimum power networks under unit cost conditions, as well as a polynomial-time one-approximation algorithm for a related Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Shortest-Paths problem. Our methods introduce a novel application of the Shapley value to calculate edge weights within F, extending upon the superfluid lemma that calculates the total weight of F. Notably, our unit-cost 4k-approximation algorithm surpasses prior best-known ratios of $8k$. A key component of our approach involves a novel sorting technique of the edges in F, followed by payment calculation using the Shapley value, that may be of independent interest. Finally, our research raises new questions regarding the minimum power network design, as well as the general k-approximation for Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths when edge costs are not identical.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation tests. Unlike other planning approaches, this method considers factors like target tracking, obstacle avoidance, and the dissemination of local data among swarm members. The approach ensures consistency across redundant computations and leverages parallel processing to optimize performance. Simulation results show that this method yields efficient and adaptable flight plans. Additionally, this framework minimizes the gap between planning and execution times, essential for real-world applications. Furthermore, it has the potential to be scalable for larger swarms. The approach has been found to reduce planning complexity from NP-complete to polynomial-time compatible with fast computation, thus suitable for real-time implementation. The code developed as part of this research has been made available online for the community's reference.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. The work sets the stage for future investigations of localized activity in network processes. The measure of nodal activity also provides new insights into critical phenomena in spreading processes. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. By leveraging advanced computer vision techniques to analyze broadcast footage, we can gain a more detailed and dynamic understanding of the game, and the value we've added to previous research in this area is reflected in the new terms we've introduced for expressing predictive probabilities of game events. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a broader analysis of broadcast location data in team sports, and its potential applications are vast. This research is part of my PhD studies at the University of Southampton, supervised by Dr. Alastair J. Wilson and Dr. Richard A. Nevill. The data used for the study was obtained from broadcast Euro 2020 and Euro 2022 matches, featuring co-locations of players' images, extracted using a state-of-the-art method, and supplemented by sports rules and common practices. Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations. Our approach has a moderate computational requirement, making it suitable for real-world applications. To facilitate future research, we are sharing our database and techniques with the community. Our database offers over 200,000 characters for training and testing, along with detailed annotations of over 1,500 characters for evaluating our relationship-determination method. Our approach has applications in archiving historical documents, improving the design of forms, and increasing the accuracy of optical character recognition (OCR). Our technique can also be adapted for contemporary forms, where OCR alone may not suffice, in scenarios like low-light image processing and documents with graphic content, following which our approach could serve as a fallback option. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. The code is openly available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/blob/master/hip_rssm.md.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we describe an outcome of asymptotic type $B$ freeness upon conditioning specific unitarily invariant random matrices. These results emerge solely from the independence and unitary invariance of the original matrices. They hold a broader significance in that they illustrate how ascertaining the properties of reduced matrices or matrices conditioned on specific parameters can be accomplished by first determining the properties of their unconditioned or unreduced counterparts. This approach is an emergent tool for analyzing matrix ensembles that have been reduced or conditioned. We include an example where an outcome of asymptotic type $B$ freeness upon conditioning yields a novel conclusion; we contend this methodology will give rise to further examples and adaptations in this domain. Ultimately, our proof of empirical spectral distribution convergence reliant solely on unitary invariance may also prove useful in instances not related to freeness. This paper is an expansion of an article initially presented at the 12th Aisenmann-Fowler Conference held in 2018. It has undergone material revisions.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of artificial networks that can be utilized for standardized testing and a publicly accessible implementation of the methods and our findings. Despite the rising concern of increased polarization in societies, our analysis indicates that many social networks lack significant structural polarization. We also introduce The Polarized Networks Dataset, which comprises artifical networks designed to exhibit varying levels of structural polarization. This dataset can be used to evaluate and compare different methods for measuring structural polarization. It is available under an open-source license at https://github.com/raffir/polarized-networks. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. If he was, this would have led to a different discussion between him and Einstein's colleague, A. Sommerfeld. As for the main mathematical issue at hand, the Einstein operator's correct parametrization is achievable when considering differential forms, making it a linear differential operator that can be expressed as the composition of the $div$ operator and the Bianchi operator. This relationship may have far-reaching implications in the study of gravitational theories. Another important result obtained from this investigation is the parameterization of the compatibility operator for the Einstein operator when considering differential modules in the context of torsion-free differential forms. This work also introduces an interesting computational method using a graphical user interface, specifically designed to visualize and determine the parametric expression of differential operators when their underlying differential modules are known. This tool's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to the Cauchy stress operator. Its source code is available for public access on reputable code repositories. Lastly, new research questions have arisen from this investigation, such as whether the Einstein operator, when considered in the context of differential forms, can be expressed as a composition of the $div$ operator and the Nijenhuis operator, a question that remains unanswered to date. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. This action is analyzed to display a certain geometric configuration among the roots, exhibiting a triangular lattice structure. A diagonalizable automorphism $s$ is constructed, and the division of the roots in $\Phi_0$ based on whether they are fixed or sent to negative roots under $s$ is described. The resulting component roots systems $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_{\omega}$ are identified as being isomorphic to the root systems of type $A_{l-1}$ and $\omega A_{l-1}$ respectively. The construction is extended to a semisimple, simply connected group $G$ based on the fundamental root system $\Phi$. The discussion also covers the creation of the group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Delta, K)$ for any subset $\Delta$ of $\Phi$. The focus then shifts to determining the maximal subgroups of type $A_l$ or $D_l$ in $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi, K)$. The relationship between the rank of the group and the number of its irreducible components as subgroups of type $A_l$ or $D_l$ is established through various contractions of root systems. Ultimately, conditions are established to guarantee the existence of a subgroup of type $A_l$ or $D_l$ in $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi, K)$. The results are validated via specific examples. In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying symmetry protection principles to describe and engineer the spontaneous emission of multi-photon bundles. Moreover, this finding facilitates the investigation of entangled photons produced through parity-preserving processes, such as electron beam parametric source or optical parametric processes, and could contribute to the development of multi-photon sources for applications in quantum technology. Lastly, this research lays the groundwork for exploring the intersection of photon bundle emission and quantum chaos in the ultrastrong coupling regime.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments conducted on various datasets, including a large social network. The algorithm's efficiency is achieved without relying on cryptographic techniques, and it can function within networks that are dynamically evolving over time. The algorithm serves as a fundamental solution that can be adaptable to addressing other crucial challenges in complex networks. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Unlike static solutions for scalar clouds, the spacetimes solved using this approach converge from multiple initial gauge choices. This new approach also exposes the intricate failure modes associated with excessive matter densities in spinning cloud configurations. As a result, this method provides a crucial tool for exploring the properties of black hole clouds surrounded by complex matter configurations. Ultimately, this method is essential for conducting a thorough investigation into the cosmological implications of such cloud formations.

A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate the existence of the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials, showcasing their unique thermal and electrical properties. Moreover, our analysis provides insights into the thermal transport behavior within these materials. Additionally, our study highlights the significance of considering both thermal and magnetic domain arrangements when analyzing the electromagnetic transport phenomena in antiferromagnetic materials. Ultimately, our research contributes valuable information for the theoretical modeling of electromagnetic transport phenomena in antiferromagnetic materials, involving a comprehensive understanding of thermal and magnetic domain factors. Our results also underscore the potential applications of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials in sustainable thermoplasmonics and spin calorometry. Lastly, our research showcases a combined experimental and theoretical approach, involving finite element modeling, for accurately measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient in complex magnetic materials. This approach can serve as a paradigm for investigating other electromagnetic transport phenomena in intricate materials. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Source code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/PILE.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As shown across four different applications, this approach allows users to integrate machine learning into their experiments with minimal modification, enabling real-time analysis that can inform and guide measurements in real time. This collaborative work between researchers and machine learning experts from various beamlines and departments aims to stimulate the development of more machine learning models and facilitate their adoption at user facilities. Furthermore, this framework serves as a starting point for creating a database of machine learning models tailored to specific measurement challenges, which can be shared across the scientific community. This initiative has the potential to give machine learning a broader presence at user facilities and pave the way for more widespread adoption in the future. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, we propose a novel tolerance-based T-time bound that accounts for both decoherence and successful ground-state achievement, offering a more comprehensive understanding of QA's dynamics. Moreover, we examine the impact of temperature on QAs failure in isolated systems, revealing that adding a thermal bath can sometimes prevent failure in isolated systems. Lastly, we propose a new decoherence-induced failure mechanism related to parity and associated with it a time-bounded diagram. This study challenges the long-held assumption that including stoquastic backgrounds improves QA's performance and instead suggests that certain types of background Hamiltonians can cause failure, a consequence stemming from the interplay between symmetry, block-diagonalization, and quantum annealing. This research is further validated through experimental implementation using quantum annealing on a D-Wave machine. The findings from this study have important implications for improving the performance of quantum annealing and may lead to a better understanding of complex quantum systems through the study of related phenomena. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Along the way, various prominent scientists encountered by the lab's directors navigated the celestial world, such as Harlow Shapley, Bertil Ohlmann, Jan Oort, and Hendrikse van Rhijn, with additional discussion on the role that the Dutch school of astronomy, led by Kapteyn and van Rhijn, played in the broader global community. Ultimately, the period from 1921 to 1957 represented a critical phase in the evolution of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, characterized by substantial growth, considerable setbacks, and ultimately, transformative change. This research is based on previously overlooked archival materials and the personal recollections of key figures who played a part in the lab's development during this time period. It is hoped that this retrospective analysis may offer valuable lessons to young researchers facing their own present-day challenges within the scientific community. It is intended that this historical review will be of interest not only to professionals within the field of astronomy but also to anyone facing analogous obstacles within their own academic discipline. It is further contemplated that this historical account may serve as a model for a broader retrospective analysis of the development of the KAP-AIP and the Leiden collections relevant to it. It is also considered that this study may be followed by additional research into specific aspects of the subject matter that have only been given a preliminary treatment here. It is finally believed that this historical review may be useful as a teaching resource for astronomy and science history courses and could be adapted to different levels of instruction.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
Furthermore, this integrated approach opens up promising avenues for optimizing composite materials with irregular damage patterns in mind. 
Ultimately, this could lead to the design of materials where detection accuracy matches their inherent ability to detect deformations and damage through conductivity changes, ultimately unlocking their full potential in critical engineering applications. 
This novel method is versatile and can be applied to various types of composite materials by integrating their unique physical properties into the algorithm. 
With minimal precision requirements for the detection method and the ability to handle complex failure patterns, this integrated approach represents a game-changer for the capable, self-sensing composite materials. 
This breakthrough paves the way for a deeper exploration of CNF's properties in relation to damage detection and could also provide insights into optimizing CNF reinforcement in composite materials, ultimately leading to more effective self-sensing materials that can accurately detect damage without additional fabrication costs. 
This approach could be particularly beneficial for applications where damage often induces significant deformations and strain, such as in aircraft and wind turbines. 
By integrating piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to accurately determine damage dimensions, a more precise understanding of CNF's property variations in relation to damage detection will be gained, leading to better optimization of CNF reinforcement in composite materials.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications. Additionally, we propose that pure knowledge learning, as opposed to learning from trial and error, is essential for collecting greater insight within groups. Finally, we propose that introducing individual intellect into collective systems is equivalent to adding a noise-reducing filter, increasing the likelihood of exploring optimal system equilibrium paths. This concept is demonstrated using simple automated systems, group learning simulations, and the complex Lotka-Volterra model. In doing so, we provide a theoretical and empirical foundation for the intellect-collective wisdom framework. This framework offers a general perspective on the relationship between individual and collective intelligence, with implications for interpreting various scientific phenomena and potentially informing practical applications. Lastly, we outline several directions for expanding this framework through empirical studies and applications. We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The key innovation is a new way to frame the problem, which translates the challenge of predicting the future into a classification problem. The system is then controlled effectively through a process of trial and error, using a technique called reinforcement learning. The algorithm works well in a wide range of scenarios, including the control of multiple interconnected systems and processes with sudden changes. The algorithm has been tested on simulation models of an aircraft in flight and a chemical reaction in a closed system, and it outperforms traditional methods in these environments. The code for the algorithm is now available for public use. The approach has the potential to make a big impact in areas like the control of robots and artificial organs. The algorithm is part of a larger project to create a computer program that can learn how to control unknown dynamical systems and share this knowledge with other robots in the real world. This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework. Following an introductory section on tensor analysis within Euclidean spaces, we demonstrate the utility of this approach by validating a range of vector integrand identities, including several previously established but lacking a comprehensive proof, several new identities, and a broader identity covering the previous ones. Consequently, this approach provides a unified explanation of these identities. Furthermore, we apply this tensor framework to derive several new vector integrand identities, along with an identity covering an extensive class of quadratic functions satisfying certain conditions, yielding specific cases that were heretofore unknown. Our method also enables the validation of a specific vector integral formula previously offered by G. Talbot. Additionally, we explore the associated volume factor within this tensor framework. Lastly, we provide a brief review of the historical development of vector integrand identities within this context. 

Keywords: Euclidean spaces, tensor analysis, vector integrand identities, vector spaces, differential geometry, vector geometry, tensor techniques.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM and NuTeV experiments and gauge the detection capabilities of the upcoming SHiP beam dump experiment which has the ability to exhaustively explore the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly. By combining all existing limits as well as the proposed SHiP sensitivity, we map out the allowable parameter space for this theoretical model, also exploring its implications for neutral current four-neuron interactions that are naturally incorporated by our model. Ultimately, we conclude that although a certain parameter scenario can explain the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly, the extent to which it falls within the allowable mass window depends on the model's parameters especially the scalar's coupling with a range that could potentially be constrained by the upcoming SHiP experiment. Moreover, we anticipate that SHiP can drastically narrow the allowable parameter space for its own four-neuron interaction scenario by at least three orders of magnitude, thereby differentiating itself from other existing or proposed experiments. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Moreover, these findings can inform the development of designed learning experiences that mitigate potential negative consequences of online learning for certain students and leverage its benefits for others. Consequently, this research offers strategies for reducing achievement gaps in online learning environments and provides a framework for exploring the interactions between learning designs and diverse student populations. Ultimately, this investigation paves the way for further research aimed at identifying specific design elements that interact with student demographics to produce these varying outcomes. By delving into the underlying causes of these demographic variations, educators can create data-driven design decisions that cater to the unique needs of each student population, leading to a more equitable learning experience. In this context, equity in online learning refers to a fair and adapted design that addresses the distinct challenges and opportunities presented by online instruction, thereby providing a comparable learning experience for all students. To this end, this research employs the label 'equity-in-design' to distinguish it from traditional conceptions of equity focused on outcome equality.
