In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
Ultimately, we contend that our intuitive four-valued logic model offers a more
appealing foundation for set theory than anticipated, warranting exploration in
its own right. This work is intended to serve as a starting point for a broader
discussion, rather than a fully developed theoretical framework. It is available
under the terms of the CC BY License.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of developing a BCI that can reliably monitor and influence an individual's gait during walking. Nonetheless, more research is needed to address the complexities of BCIs in real-world scenarios, such as varying walking speeds and environments, and implementing systems for over longer periods without a break. Still, this study represents a significant step forward for the development of BCI-powered lower limb prosthetics, especially for recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. To this end, a prototype of a hybrid brain-prosthetic controller was built, combining the BCI system with commercial prosthetic control technology to demonstrate its effectiveness in a feasibility study with two subjects. The results showed that this system can accurately control the forward and backward movement of a hip joint actuator attached to a lower limb, thus offering a viable solution for safe and reliable lower limb prosthetic control. This breakthrough could also contribute to a deeper understanding of the brain's control mechanisms behind walking and may have implications for the treatment of walking disorders caused by abnormal brain function. Lastly, the data collected can be utilized for further training and validation of computational brain models used for studying the neural basis of locomotion. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the capabilities of high-resolution ECoG recordings in accurately decoding the most complex aspects of gait in healthy individuals and provides a solid foundation for developing safe and reliable lower limb prosthetic control systems, especially for recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Additionally, we demonstrate that for a right-angled Artin group whose minimal action on a tree includes a non-trivial, periodic orbit, its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts periodically on an edge of the tree. Furthermore, we show that if a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree has a non-trivial, minimal action and its graph $\Gamma$ has no component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree, then its minimal action on a tree is highly transitive. Lastly, we provide an example to illustrate that there exists a right-angled Artin group whose minimal action on a tree is highly transitive but has a non-trivial, periodic orbit. This example stems from a graph that recently appeared in a different context. 

This research is an extension of questions posed by Minha Roy in her paper titled "Right-Angled Artin Groups and Tree Automorphisms." 

Keywords: right-angled Artin groups, group actions on trees, highly transitive groups. 

This article is part of the edited collection for the 21st Ontario-MacDonald Conference in Group Theory, held in Toronto, Canada, from August 16 to August 19, 2019.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. We showcase DECENNT's effectiveness on multiple tasks: predicting neural oscillatory patterns, identifying directing relationships in multimodal networks, and decoding critical time frames in time series data. We hope DECENNT to serve as a model for further research on dynamic graph neural networks. The code is available at https://github.com/aciman/DECENNT.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. Furthermore, we investigate how different retention rules, type of roots, and number of reticulations influence the accuracy of these networks in mimicking real-world data. Additionally, we undertake a comparative assessment of six distinct network reconstruction methods by evaluating the precision and recall of these methods in identifying real reticulations from a curated dataset consisting of 20 species. Throughout our study, we make available a comprehensive set of results in the form of a dataset that can be utilized for comparing future network generators and reconstruction methods. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed approach and associated dataset have the potential to contribute to several important computer vision challenges, including action recognition, object detection, and tracking. In addition, biolocomotion detection may also enhance the effectiveness of video analysis in applications related to wildlife conservation. The code, dataset, and experiments described in this document are available online at https://github.com/ashish3624/Biolocomotion-Detection. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. A Python implementation of NN is provided, demonstrating its convergence and offering a faster alternative to classic direct inversion for large matrices. In particular, NN outperforms classic direct inversion for matrices above 10G dimensions on a single GPU, and can be an effective method for matrix inversion in positive definite matrices, particularly those with low spectral norm, and general linear systems, including sparse systems, where further research on sparse NN is warranted. The code is compatible with the PyTorch library and can be run on a single GPU. The code has been successfully tested on the P100, V100, and A100 GPUs. The code is available online at https://github.com/zheng0625/Nested-Neumann. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. This research is relevant to current experiments involving synthetic and natural one-dimensional systems with nonmagnetic disorders.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research is grounded in the context of harmonic sums and their relation to polylogarithms, and it explores the extension of this relationship to higher genus curves and its potential implications for the computation of multi-loop Feynman integrals. The study concludes with an examination of future directions, including the potential application of genus one geometry to broaden the scope of computational harmonic sum calculations and the exploration of higher genus curves in relation to multiple polylogarithms. The research is also expected to contribute to the further development of geometric approaches in computational multi-loop physics. The study presents novel results in the form of genus one curve summaries, isogeny diagrams, and computational harmonic sum tables, and it offers an overview of the currently employed geometric approach in computational multi-loop physics, including the application of the Baikov parameters system in its comprehensive form. The research has been made publicly accessible through the provided reference list and the attached curve databases. The investigation is part of an ongoing project to thoroughly compute two-loop harmonic sum integrals, and it paves the way for the exploration of higher genus curves in relation to multiple polylogarithms. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. An implementation of the test is integrated into the R package 'jetm'. Alongside, an empirical analysis is conducted using US election data. This analysis is combined with theoretical results to demonstrate the test's efficacy in detecting non-linear relationships in autoregressive models. Overall, the proposed test offers a valuable tool for investigating linearity in complex network autoregressive models. The code for the test and empirical analysis has been made publicly available. Recent work introduced deep declarative networks as a framework that treats various differentiation rules as a representation for a given problem's solution set. This approach has been particularly effective in applying and interpreting complex mathematical concepts within deep learning models. In this study, we expand on this framework by reinterpreting the optimization problems it addresses in the context of variational inequalities and differential complementarity problems. By differentiating the implicit equations that define these problems, we derive a method for computing gradients through an equivalent optimization problem. This technique enables us to incorporate external constraints and optimization algorithms into the original variational inequalities. As a result, we can now incorporate external constraints and optimization algorithms into the original variational inequalities. As a result, we can now incorporate learning algorithms that utilize the optimal solution sets of the problems, rather than the problems themselves, as training data. This is particularly relevant in applications where only sample solutions are available. In our analysis, we demonstrate that the resulting deep declarative networks preserve their differentiability properties. To facilitate practical implementations, we provide an open-source library that incorporates an efficient C++ solver for each iteration's optimization problem. This efficient C++ solver for each iteration's optimization problem is encapsulated in a PyTorch module, which leverages the performance benefits of just-in-time compilation (JIT) while ensuring seamless integration with Python-based deep learning workflows. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a real-world problem involving the optimization of camera networks for monitoring crowd levels. The optimization problem in this scenario involves finding the optimal solution set that minimizes a monitoring error function, where the derivative of this function is now computed using the deep declarative network. The results show that this approach produces high-quality solutions that closely match the true optimal solutions, as validated through rigorous mathematical analysis and comparisons with state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms. Moreover, this method achieves significant performance improvements in both simulation environments and real-world deployments. The code for this research is available online. Despite its efficiency, the model's accuracy and computational efficiency can be improved even further. Future directions for enhancement are also identified and presented. This research is relevant to multiple fields of study and has the potential to be applied to a broad spectrum of optimization problems that involve variational inequalities. Moreover, its data representation innovations have the potential to be applied to multiple data sets that have an associated optimization problem, such as those listed within the MMIST dataset, which is also explored in this research. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed approach offers various simplification levels and has been validated through experimentation with immortalized keratinocytes and cancer cells. Notably, it has been observed that cancer cells often follow the same spreading mechanism but with speed adjustment due to increased cytoskeletal mobility, ultimately leading to irregular movements. This suggests that cytoskeletal impassability could be a crucial factor in shaping cellular spreading patterns, especially in tighter environments. This framework has the potential to be applied to various other cellular spreading scenarios by adapting its parameters and simplification levels. This numerical methodology can be augmented with stochastic elements to model future developments in cellular research, such as the influence of filaments on protein membrane movement or the effects of coiled coils on keratin fiber interactions. Overall, our multi-scale framework offers a comprehensive tool for investigating cellular spreading and locomotion, encompassing a range of phenomena influenced by internal constituent interactions and external stimuli. This approach has the potential to be an invaluable resource for the field of computational cellular biology, enabling researchers to better understand intricate cellular behaviors and inform related engineering applications. This methodology is now available as an open-source code on https://github.com/CMU-BIOS/CellSpreading for the benefit of the scientific community. This code can be used in tandem with the framework's documentation, located at https://cmu-bios.github.io/CellSpreading/, to replicate the results presented in this study and explore new scenarios. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. By uncovering hidden patterns in temporal transaction graphs, our research paves the way for further exploration of blockchain security and money trail analysis. In the future, we intend to enhance our techniques for real-time detection and prevention of malicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these deepQ learning decoders could be learned through interaction with virtual code environments, operated directly on real hardware without additional training, and matched the performance of leading classical decoding algorithms like MINIDEC and repeated shrinkage. Additionally, we found that incorporating the process of readout error correction, previously deemed insurable, could be handled efficiently by our decoder. Finally, we explored the decoding of channels with moving noise locations, a critical capability for real-time performance in large-scale quantum systems. While we achieved some success with this challenge, we also identified several possible paths for improving code learning through the application of alternative reinforcement learning techniques. This initial exploration of learning surface code decoding strategies lays the groundwork for a broader investigation into the potential for code learning to address fundamental challenges in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. The medium's response in Au$+$Au collisions is characterized by an enhanced correlation at large angles, representing an additional contribution of up to 35% of observed hadrons in this region. These results provide evidence that the medium creates hadrons beyond the fragmentation of charged particles, implying that the charged component significantly underestimates hadron production in heavy ion collisions. Additionally, an increased yield of hadrons with lower momentum fractions suggests an additional mechanism involving the interaction between the medium and hadron mass, possibly related to the discovery of hadron mass in quantum chromodynamics. Lastly, an examination of the excess yield as a function of collision system, rather than hadron type, reveals a continuous trend from $p$$+$$p$ to Au$+$Au via $d$$+$Au and $d$$+Au$ collisions, demonstrating that the observed phenomenon is a continuous effect of cold nuclear matter and systemic response of the medium in heavy ion collisions. A scalar quantity representing the medium's response in Au$+$Au collisions is $0.035\pm0.014$ of the observed hadron yield in this $p_T$ range. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of software companies. The findings indicate that adopting home-based Scrum meetings reduces flexibility in meetings, but enhances satisfaction with meetings. Moreover, it identifies key factors influencing these outcomes. Interestingly, working from home was found to increase the satisfaction with Scrum meetings, but seemed to counterintuitively diminish flexibility in meetings. A further analysis revealed that this counterintuitive effect could be attributed to individuals being less willing to adjust their working schedules to accommodate colleagues once they are at home. A review of existing literature offered possible explanations for this reluctance, suggesting it may stem from the difficulty of separating work and personal life at home, leading to a tendency to prioritize individual goals over collaborative flexibility. To enhance employee well-being in remote working setups, it is imperative to support their autonomy, relatedness, and competence. Possible strategies to achieve this include adopting results-oriented work environments and providing employees with the flexibility to manage their time freely. A review of existing literature also indicated that home-based Scrum meetings may require adjustments to culture, meeting structure, and technology to prevent distractions and difficulties in real-time communication. In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights for companies operating in the software sector, highlighting the need to strike a balance between individual freedom and collaborative flexibility in home-based Scrum setups to optimize performance and employee well-being. A theoretical framework proposed in this article offers companies a useful tool for designing effective strategies to achieve this balance. A review of existing literature indicated that this balance is critical to supporting employees' autonomy, relatedness, and competence in remote working setups, and several possible strategies were identified for achieving this balance, such as adopting results-oriented work environments and providing employees with the freedom to manage their time freely. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Various models, including those with initial condition anisotropies and temperature dependencies, struggle to fully capture our observations.  Specifically, models fail to accurately replicate the relationship between event-shape and flow in different centrality ranges.  Still, most models successfully recreate the event-shape selection's impact on the $v_2$/$v_4$ ratio.  Also found is that the elliptic flow coefficient increases with collision energy in 5.02 TeV collisions, whereas 2.76 TeV collisions exhibit an opposite trend.  Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the event-shape selection's influence on the $v_2$/$v_4$ ratio is unaffected by collision energy.  Additional analysis, encompassing higher-order flow and different particle species, reveals that the event-shape selection's impact is directly proportional to initial anisotropy.  Consequently, our results reinforce the utility of the Event Shape Engineering method in distinguishing between nuclear density and temperature-dependent physics.  Also, our results within mid-central collisions demonstrate that radial and elliptic flow phenomena share a common underlying cause.  Finally, our results within high-centrality collisions suggest that initial condition anisotropies play a minimal role in higher-order flow.  This research is based on data acquired with the ALICE detector at the LHC.  Specifically, it utilizes data from 7 billion events collected for proton-proton collisions and 16 billion events collected for lead-lead collisions.  Several theoretical models are compared to our results, including iEBE-VISHNU, iMB, AMPT, and MUSIC.  Additionally, our results are further contextualized with various other experimental outcomes, including those from the LHC and RHIC.  Finally, this research is presented in an abstract that will be shared at the Quark Matter 2019 conference.  Corresponding authors of this research include Steven J. Lee and Jihun Lee. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step integration algorithm is an efficient and accurate solution for simulating long-term sediment transport with numerous particles. Our code is now available for public use.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. Additionally, the minimum value of $n$ is investigated, and it is found that the smallest possible value is $3$. Furthermore, the number of distinct pairs $(a,b)$ can be any value greater than $1$ for any given value of $n$ between $3$ and $6$. A common generation method is proposed for any given $n$. A link is established between the factors of the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ and the powers of a certain polynomial over finite fields, known as the factor field construction. A specific case is examined where this construction is applied to a specific polynomial, known as the Frobenius automorphism, and its connection to the Galois groups of polynomials with a specific format is explored. Finally, this research is linked to another recent study, and several open questions are posed.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached a height of 14.3cm, 87% of the desired height, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed control system in the presence of soft ground deformation. Additionally, the impact of model inaccuracy, foot size, and grain size on the robot's performance was explored, showcasing the feedback controller's capacity to adapt to different conditions while propagating errors through the feedback loop. To further validate the feedback controller's performance, it was applied to a physical robot jumping on a soft surface, comprised of 10-kg bags of rice, and successfully achieved 80% of the desired height. The findings from the simulation and real-world tests revealed the feedback controller's ability to compensate for model inaccuracy and other factors contributing to ground reaction force variability. Consequently, the developed feedback controller can be applied to a broader range of ground conditions. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. As we continue to observe substantial performance gaps between human communication standards and current NLP models, our CONDAQA dataset represents a crucial step towards creating more capable models that can accurately process negation within language. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Notably, in scenarios where the annealing gap is negligible, shallow quantum annealing trials yield acceptable solution percentages. Additionally, in scenarios where the annealing gap is significant, deep quantum annealing trials significantly improve solution-finding probability, albeit at the cost of precious resources. Deep, understanding the dynamics of shallow quantum annealing trials is, therefore, an indispensable prerequisite for strategic quantum annealing planning. While neural networks can speed up understanding, even in an unsupervised scenario, they are particularly useful in complex case scenarios where the annealing gap is significant, defined as instances where the fidelity of the ground state at the annealing end point exceeds 0.5. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Includes discussions on the limitations of these one-band models as compared to
their multi-band counterparts. 
Also, a discussion on the total weight distribution across all bands as a more
applicable benchmark to assess one-band model validity. 
Lastly, the necessity to consider a sufficient number of bands with careful
weight distribution across them is emphasized, given the complexity of the
Hamiltonian at hand. 
All theoretical model derivations and discussions are set within the context of
recent experimental studies on the electronic structure of infinite layered
nickelates. 
Additionally, the screening factors obtained are compared to those measured
experimentally. 
Furthermore, a comparison is drawn between calculated weight distribution
patterns and those obtained through first principle band structure calculations. 
All necessary steps for self-docking an infinite layered nickelate model are
outlined. 
All corresponding one-band models are solved for their ground states and the
results compared against each other.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Lastly, this research identifies an accelerated decay process in the context of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. Almost uniform phase mixing estimates are also established, and in the context of observable quantities, this results in a uniform bound on decay rates influenced by Landau damping and dispersive processes, as well as an accelerated decay process, for the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation, driven by the Taylor dispersion process. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry. When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Concrete results
show our method provides accurate role assignments for both small and large software
systems, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we explore methods for
adaptively calculating optimal calculation batches, but they may not always yield
the best results. Our implementation, including source code and data sets, is
available online. Conclusion and related work discuss implications of our approach
and potential areas for further development.

However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We demonstrate the applicability of our findings to solve maximum-weight Tai mapping through integer programming by cutting plane method, a widely used optimization technique, and discuss its limitations and potential improvements. We conclude by suggesting new research directions related to the anti Tai mapping concept. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. Ultimately, this model suggests that dust development and settling may suppress VSI's presence further out in protoplanetary disks, aligning with observational data and offering a possible explanation for particle distribution patterns observed in certain systems, including HL Tau and a T Tauri disk system. The components of this research could be applied to a broader range of stability problems involving layered systems in protoplanetary disks. The effects of gas flow on particle development and settling also warrant additional research in various protoplanetary disk configurations. The presented model is compatible with the DUSTDEV model, focusing solely on its interactions with VSI. The modified VSI model, accompanied by a theoretical analysis, is now part of the DUSTDEV framework along with its results on particle development and settling in various protoplanetary disk environments. The code for this research has been made publicly accessible for further use and adaptation. The code can be found at https://github.com/alexmiller2706/VSI-sdust along with the parameters employed in the presented figures and potential future applications of the model. Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. A potential experimental realization of these self-accelerating solitons could be achieved using $^{87}$Rb atomic condensates and optical-lattice traps by manipulating resolvable energy levels. This finding is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of non-linear physics and its unique self-accelerating modes. This research is also expected to lead to the development of more sophisticated optical-lattice-based models, ultimately paving the way for the realization of other hypothetical self-accelerating modes in other linear and non-linear systems. This could potentially result in the generation of self-accelerating modes in optical-lattice-based models, even those involving different types of particles, such as photons in coupled waveguides, atomic-matterwaves in optical waveguides, and electrons in electric-layers. This could be achieved by mapping the potentials and interactions in these systems to those described by the two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, we have open-sourced the SIMC 2.0 framework and conducted a comprehensive evaluation on popular ML models, including support vector machines, neural networks, and deep neural networks. Additionally, we have successfully applied the SIMC 2.0 protocol to a real-world dataset, achieving a runtime of under 14 milliseconds on a single GPU. Moreover, our analysis reveals multiple opportunities for further optimization and considers the interplay between coding techniques and other ML protocols. Ultimately, SIMC 2.0 is anticipated to serve as a pivotal stepping stone towards developing efficient and scalable private ML systems. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of a massive tail discovered in both optical and HI observations within M101's central region. In this work, various interactions between the HI disk and its associated galaxies are analyzed using collisionless N-body simulations. These simulations last for a time period of 10 billion years and consider a variety of scenarios, including both direct and gravitational interactions between the galaxies and the HI disk. In doing so, this research provides a visual representation of how interactions affect the HI disk's structure and help clarify the origins of the various HI features observed around M101. In this context, detecting an irregular HI disk around a galaxy like M101 can indicate ongoing interactions with nearby galaxies. In such cases, further optical and HI surveys should focus on identifying visible counterparts to HI clouds and tails, analyzing their shapes, sizes, and spectral characteristics to better comprehend the galaxy interactions involved. In this research, we provide a visual representation of how interactions between the HI disk and its associated galaxies affect their structures through collisionless N-body simulations, providing a framework for comparing observed and predicted HI tail shapes. In this work, various scenarios are considered where the galaxy and its companion interact with the HI disk, including (a) a direct gravitational interaction between the galaxy and the HI disk, (b) an indirect gravitational interaction between the galaxy and the HI disk, and (c) a collision between the galaxy and the HI disk

The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This method is particularly concise and straightforward in global number domains, where it merely involves repeatedly using the Frobenius endomorphism and mapping between domains, without needing an explicit computation of the integral. Our method also establishes a new understanding of a fundamental theorem attributed to Nesterenko and Corvaya, by demonstrating that the algebraic closure of a global domain is equivalent to the set of elements that can be expressed as the sum of two squared components, or as the product of two elements with specific properties. This discovery, in turn, leads to several additional notable outcomes, including a new proof of a result related to Scholz Conjecture, as well as the ability to establish the field of rational functions over a global domain as a Hilbert field. All the new results derived in this study are proven applicable to number domains and global function domains alike. Furthermore, we present an independent proof for the ability to divide any element of a global domain into the sum of two squared components, using an advanced method involving the Galois group and field extensions, with a scope limited to number domains only. This development is however distinct from our primary method described above. As a collective effort, these findings provide a comprehensive framework for handling expressions of positive elements as sums of squared components across a wide range of domains and fields. This leads to further outcomes, including an independent proof of the Scholz Conjecture, with the additional result that this technique can be extended to cover fields of rational functions over number domains or global function domains. This means that in such domains, we now have not just the application of this method, but also the associated outcomes derived from it. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This method is adaptable to different graph topologies and learning processes. Moreover, our results show that this algorithm produces efficient node samples, leading to faster model convergence and lower biases during a cancer data set classification task. The algorithm's performance is also evaluated on an artificial data set with a complex graph structure. This research is an initial exploration of applying meta-learning to solve federated learning challenges. The developed algorithms and theory are a crucial step towards tackling other problems involving distributed data sets. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Moreover, the ability of turbulent flows to overcome stable geostrophic vortices was found to depend critically on the level of rotational shear within the system. Additionally, the occurrence of stable geostrophic vortices was found to be highly non-stationary, with an extremely slow evolution rate that is significantly influenced by the formation and dissolution of stable waves. In contrast, wave turbulence was found to evolve at a much faster rate, with an evolution time that is directly proportional to the square of the Rossby number. These non-stationary properties of turbulent flows were found to be governed by a new triple timescale model. The model includes a fast cascade phase, a intermediate phase characterized by the coexistence of stable waves and turbulence, and a very slow phase of stationary state. The viability of this model is validated through various statistical tests, including the application of the Kolmogorov entropy to distinguish between stationary and non-stationary states. Moreover, the analysis of the frequency spectrum within the triply periodic box case reveals the emergence of a majorette peak, which is a harmonic frequency component of the inertial wave frequency. The occurrence of this peak is found to be a clear indicator of the presence of stable waves within the system. The bi-stability theory is further supported by the application of the varialbe multiscaling technique, which reveals a significant shift in the scaling exponents from a value of 2 to a value of 3 when moving from the stable wave state to the wave turbulence state. The triply periodic box case is found to exhibit a unique multiscaling curve that displays a distinct two-fold symmetry, which is a direct consequence of the competition between the two frequency components, the primary frequency component and the majorette frequency component, which are both separated by an odd multiple of $\pi$ in the frequency space

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Our results demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the algorithm achieves a convergence rate of $O(1/T)$, with influences from the FedBuff framework, differential privacy, and delayed updates. To validate the algorithm's performance, we conduct comprehensive experiments involving numerical data sets and real-world image data sets, showcasing its enhanced efficiency and reliability. Comparisons with leading baselines, including FedAvg and SFB, highlight the modified FedBuff algorithm's superiority in terms of efficiency and convergence rate. Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. Moreover, the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ spectrum, where $\rho^0(1450)$ cannot contribute due to Bose-Einstein statistics, is accounted for by an $S$-wave contribution alone.  The theoretical estimates of branching fractions and/or direct $CP$ asymmetries for $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$, $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ and $B^0 \to K^0 K^- K^+$ decays are presented for verification with upcoming experiments at LHCb and Belle-II.  Therefore, we recommend experimental validation through a more precise analysis of relevant data by these research colleagues.  Additionally, the theoretical models that describe the $\rho^0(1450)$ state can be tested with our proposed research approach. Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter. Conditions are also identified under which the abundance of such black holes remains consistent with existing gravitational wave background experiments. Finally, we examine how an additional dimension affects the evolution of primordial black holes in multiverse scenarios inspired by eternal inflation, finding that their abundance is influenced by the number of universes that branch off from each black hole-creating collision, for example. We propose that future gravitational wave observatories may identify the signature of primordial black holes if they have a fraction of the dark matter share and collaborate with gamma-ray observatories to pinpoint their presence. The effect of an additional dimension also slows down the formation of primordial black holes in multiverse scenarios, which may increase their abundance as a result. We also discover that primordial black holes have a tendency to concentrate on overdensity regions, which enhances their formation, unlike typical scalar perturbations. Finally, we propose that future experiments, such as LISA, should look for the impact of primordial black holes on the formation of the cosmic large-scale structure when assuming a substantial fraction of the dark matter share. This could involve modeling the effect of primordial black holes' gravitational influence on typical matter fluctuations and incorporating these models into numerical codes that simulate the evolution of the cosmos. The availability of an additional dimension also raises the possibility of solving the cosmological singularity problem through a quantum gravity-driven collapse of a cylical universe, where a primordial black hole's formation plays a key role. This research provides a foundation for a deeper scientific investigation into the interconnections between an additional dimension, primordial black holes, and the Swampland program, which includes dark energy's scarcity, a stable gravitational wave background, the possibility of dark matter consisting of primordial black holes, and the singularity problem

Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also helps us understand that by controlling the rate of expansion, we can switch from a breakdown pattern dominated by the forces of expansion, to one that is dominated by the forces of surface tension and viscosity. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. Additionally, we found lower bounds on the space required for sorting networks with constant depth, which are comparable to our findings on comparator arity. We also explored upper bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with n inputs and varying depth. We found that k is equal to n^(log2(n)/log2(4)) up to n = 4096. We also found that k is equal to O(n^0.301) up to n = 4096. Furthermore, we found that k is equal to O(n^0.264) up to n = 512 and n = 1024. We believe these results provide valuable insights into the relationships between comparator arity, number of inputs, and depth in sorting networks. Moreover, we hope our research will contribute to the ongoing study of lower bounds in circuit complexity theory. Additionally, our research may lead to the development of comparative analysis for other comparators with multiple input values. Lastly, our research could result in the identification of lower bounds on comparator arity for other problems beyond sorting networks. We present a series of sorting networks with constant depth to illustrate our findings. We also explore open questions and possible directions for future research. Lastly, we offer a companion repository containing our circuits from a previous study.
