Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like shapes. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations, effectively impacting gas dynamics. This findings are further supported by visualizations of magnetic field strength and density, revealing complex patterns forming around merging galaxy cores and contributing to enhanced star formation through winding and collapsing gas structures. Ultimately, this study suggests that magnetic fields play a significant role in shaping galaxy morphology, especially in abundant gas scenarios.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, the proposed method proves beneficial for adapting to domains where there is some unlabeled data available. The code and models are openly accessible for replication and further development at this link https://github.com/ghruvos/meta-gec.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating the impact of rounding errors to some extent. However, the overall approach highlights the significance of data precision in statistics and the need for caution when interpreting rounded figures. particularly in tracking rare events. The developed measures can also be adapted for mitigation strategies in other data sensitivity scenarios.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, this fairness condition holds in an even weaker form, known as one-good maximin share fairness. Through our investigation, we opened up new research avenues, especially concerning the identification of mechanisms that always result in pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX or EF1 allocations for any number of agents. Additionally, we offered a new definition of fairness, known as X-good fairness, where X represents any good up to some arbitrary number. Lastly, we offered a method that produces pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations for two agents, although it is not efficient in a non-selfish setting. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The code for our method has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NFAU. The paper's findings have been published in the proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV 2023).

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The relative brightness of the outer star clusters in UGC 8839 allows for a measurement of the distance to the galaxy, which is found to be approximately 139 million light-years. The large angular diameter of UGC 8839, approximately 72, presents a significant challenge for predicting its mass based on its disk size. The predicted mass of UGC 8839, an intrinsic measure of a galaxy's gravitational influence, is unusually low for a spiral galaxy of its size. The unique characteristics of UGC 8839 make it an interesting subject for studies of dwarf galaxies and candidates for dark matter detection. The galaxy's thin disk and lack of prominent bars, rings, or tidal features make it a suitable comparison object for massive spiral galaxies. The optical image of UGC 8839 is accompanied by a high-resolution X-ray image from Chandra, showing the extensive hot gas surrounding the galaxy and suggesting a link between the gas and the galaxy's dark matter disk. The X-ray image also reveals a large tail of hot gas extending from the galaxy's disk, possibly associated with a interaction between UGC 8839 and a nearby galaxy. The X-ray data, combined with optical observations, provide the first evidence of a large-scale stellar stream associated with UGC 8839. The galaxy's unique features, notable star formation in the extreme outer rim and low surface brightness inside it, make it an interesting subject for studies of the stability of galaxy disks and the detection of dark matter. Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential. Theoretical feasibility of DP-Sync is demonstrated through practical implementations, including encrypted photo collections and online datasets encrypted with SQL. The DP-Sync framework provides robust protection against various attacks, including those on update patterns, data, and classification, without compromising query efficiency, proving itself to be both secure and practical. The source code for DP-Sync is available online.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ghushy/RF-EXplain. The comprehensive study of this topic remains an area of additional research, and we hope our work serves as a catalyst for similar explanations in ML models like Neural Networks.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by high Dice coefficients and fast frame rates, signifies significant potential for its application in medical tool tracking. Moreover, our model's ease of training and minimal loss made it an attractive solution for solving this complex problem. Additionally, the code and model are freely available online for the benefit of industry professionals and researchers in the field. Nonetheless, further improvements in robustness and testing in real-world environments are needed to facilitate safe adoption in clinical settings.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model weights available to the public, we aim to stimulate the development of more advanced methods for learning from unlabeled video content.

This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. Results demonstrate the capability of the new framework to achieve competitive accuracy compared to established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models. Consequently, the paper suggests that the proposed model could be a viable alternative for forecasting financial risk variables. Nonetheless, it is recommended to conduct further research in order to adjust the model for accommodative parameter settings. The new framework's website is available at https://github.com/ChoiJinhyun/Realized-ThresGARCH, where users can locate code repositories and conduct their own replication tests. Moreover, the paper's data sets utilized in the practical study have been uploaded to https://data.taiwan.edu.tw/, categorized as 'Stock market volatility forecasting'. Lastly, the paper's code repository includes a sample dataset available at https://github.com/ChoiJinhyun/Realized-ThresGARCH/tree/main/Extras. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Our studies aim to provide insights into the internal structure of the pion. Despite being an elementary particle consisting of two quarks, the pion exhibits unique properties that distinguish it from other hadrons, rendering it an interesting subject of study within the field of quantum chromodynamics. Consequently, understanding the quark's internal dynamics will contribute significantly to a more comprehensive grasp of hadron physics. A total of 22 distinct combinations of quark masses were examined across three different ensembles, with mass values ranging from the charm quark's mass to being nearly equal to its mass. To remove any ambiguity in the measurement process, the latent time was set at 0.5 times the lattice's Thomas range. Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects. Furthermore, our analysis of XX Cha reveals that its
mass accretion variability is linked to changes in its stellar rotation period,
along with a possible connection to long-period variations in its spectral
line positions, both of which are likely influenced by the star's interacting
magnetic field and wind. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of
accounting for mass accretion variability when interpreting observations of
protoplanetary disks, and they also motivate the need for a more in-depth
analysis of mass accretion variability in a broader sample of T Tauri stars.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. The DataScope framework is applicable to a broad range of machine learning pipelines and its efficient computation of the Shapley value for training examples paves the way for the development of more advanced data debugging techniques. The system's source code is available online. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. The validity of our methods is verified through numerical simulation and comparative analysis with cross-sectional near-field images. Furthermore, we demonstrate that entropy can differentiate between first-order transverse modes and reflect the impact of microcavity shape and loss on emission directionality. Ultimately, our approach provides a versatile and effective means of analyzing the complex far-field patterns encountered in microcavity lasers.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Further, it's shown that increased performance is directly linked to the efficacy of the GMM codebook technique. Unlike other approaches, no assumption about array calibration or ideal feedback is made; rather, a focus on improving performance with limited pilot data transmission is prioritized. A comparative study of different codebook designs based on GMMs is also presented, showcasing their variations' performance. Finally, findings are validated through numerical results and real-world trials. Additionally, this research is applicable to a range of wireless communication systems, including multiuser massive MIMO systems, where all users share the same resource blocks, and a central finding that enhanced performance is directly linked to the efficacy of the GMM codebook technique can be applied more broadly. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Despite the challenges posed by noisy quantum operations, we find that MSQITE can be an effective tool for quantum state simulations. However, further research is needed to fully assess its theoretical limits. Our source code is available for open modification and use via GitHub. https://github.com/lmiao22/MSQITE.git

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. Consequently, we conclude that in equidimensional excellent local rings, the condition $R \geq 2$ is sufficient for $F$-rationality, which is supported by existing research. Finally, we introduce a generalization of the upper bound for the tight Hilbert function, making this generalized upper bound applicable to various types of rings. It is also demonstrated that without the equidimensional constraint, the ring's $F$-rationality is not guaranteed, as indicated by constructed examples. Lastly, we propose a conjecture that a specific polynomial is non-negative over all excellent local rings. This conjecture is confirmed for equidimensional excellent local rings and is supported by existing research. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and its methodology are available for download at https://github.com/ai-economics/MESA-PyPSA. The code includes the design issue and data set used in this research. The model and its methodology are also openly published in the paper's accompanying repository at https://osf.io/7d4dw/. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. The underlying idea of combining fields and group actions may also be expanded to cover various contexts, including number fields and abelian varieties. To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency. Additionally, we investigated the impact of enhancing the energy of the LHC to 100 TeV, increasing the signal efficiency to $0.68\%$ background suppression. To optimize low background contamination below the irreducible top quark pair background threshold, we explored alternative approaches using variable order top quark decays and Higgs-assisted background suppression techniques. With these methods, even a $0.004\%$ background suppression, corresponding to a $13\%$ Higgs boson pair efficiency at $100 \textrm{TeV}$, can be achieved. However, this would require additional research on detector performance and background suppression techniques. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates the feasibility of studying non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method and suggests that searching for non-resonant Higgs boson pair production may be viable at the LHC, even at 100 TeV, although it poses significant methodological challenges. To facilitate further research, we have made the analysis code publicly available.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The vortex in the north was also found to be surrounded by clouds consisting of CO2 and water ice and was influenced by a retrograding polar jet that was formed in the spring. The retrograding jet slowed down the vortex's formation and caused it to take on a hexagonal shape. The vortex in the north began to break down in the early fall, and by the end of the year it had disappeared. The retrograding jet accelerated in the fall and eventually caught up with the vortex that had broken apart from the increasing wind speeds. The vortex in the south exhibited the same characteristics as the one in the north but formed later in the spring and disappeared faster in the winter. The vortex in the south was also surrounded by a temperature gradient at 68 degrees latitude. The formation of these polar vortices is a result of the combination of the gravitational influence of the three moons closest to Saturn, the retrograding of the polar jet, and the presence of the south polar vortex that serves as a template for the formation of the north polar vortex. The dissolution of these vortices is a result of the combination of the absorption of wave energy and the movement of air from the equator towards the poles. The study of the polar vortices in Saturn provides a basis for comparison with the study of the polar vortices in the Earth's atmosphere. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach also allows us to demonstrate the optimal blow-up criterion under the same conditions mentioned above. Our method is also adaptable for extensions of this problem to an arbitrary domain. However, in this case, we are constrained by non-optimal blow-up criteria, relying on energy bounds near boundary points. Consequently, we are able to establish a lower bound for the approach to blow-up within this context. A further discussion is also presented to address potential applications and related issues. Due to technical limitations, we are unable to accommodate additional boundary conditions in this framework. Consequently, this approach is applicable to solutions subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, where the influence of boundary conditions is minimal, given the current formulation. Nonetheless, we are confident that this approach has the potential to yield more definitive results in scenarios where additional boundary conditions hold greater significance. Lastly, we touch upon potential avenues for further investigation, including possible extensions to the Klein-Gordon equation and the exploration of modified variance measures in related contexts. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation between electrons, with the effect of these interactions playing a pivotal role in determining the transition's occurrence.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the significance of factoring in surface-related effects while interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics.  Our research provides a novel perspective on the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films, offering a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the necessity of factoring in surface-related effects when interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the effect of free carriers on spectral weight distribution, a universal phenomenon observable across all materials, from metals to insulators, with a specific focus on V$_2$O$_3$ films undergoing metal-insulator transition. Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions should be described by a more accurate approach, such as the one provided by microscopically exact time-dependent numerics. Finally, we predict that in quantum double dark-soliton systems, noise in local density measurements should exhibit an unusual periodic variation, related to the generation of antiparticles that occur when atoms move between the dark core and the surrounding 'light' regions. This antiparticle generation leads to a periodic variation in the local density at specific locations along the chain. We believe that this phenomenon of antiparticle noise could be an early sign of a more complex non-equilibrium phase of matter. We validate our findings by comparing our exact time-dependent calculations to numerical solutions of the Bogoliubov approach. However, in stronger-coupling scenarios, our exact results reveal a more intricate structure in the noise spectrum that is not captured by the Bogoliubov approach. We anticipate that this discovery will contribute to a fresh understanding of the dynamics of strong-interaction boson gases. This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3. This understanding reveals a direct relationship between the geometric measure of orbits and Weyl's orbital integrals, as expressed through the action of these groups on complex projective spaces. This insight enables a straightforward derivation of measures normalizing orbital integrals in these cases. We also establish the extension of this measure normalization to real reductive groups through the fundamental correspondence of complex groups. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this normalization to beyond endoscopy in the GL2 category, presenting an extension of Langlands' Beyond Endoscopy conjecture to include orbital integrals. This extension is formulated as a new problem tailored to the underlying mathematical framework, specifically within the context of Gelbart's and Langlands' contributions. This discussion may contribute to clarifying technical aspects of research, particularly in relation to the works of Altug, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Kirillov. We also hope to contribute to advancing research in this area by providing a accessible explanation of these concepts and measures, along with a proposed extension of the Langlands Program. This informal note is intended to offer a starting point for further research in this complex field of mathematics. We have a proposed extension of the Langlands Program, but we acknowledge that this idea requires thorough examination and validation by expert researchers in the field. We look forward to following the development of this new problem and the associated research in the future. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, this technique may be extended to different types of measurements and various types of light-matter interactions. As a result, we were able to measure the mixing ratio of electric-dipole allowed transitions to magnetic-dipole transitions in highly excited iron-57 nuclei and show the application of this technique for improving the measurement of spectral lines in x-ray spectra. This approach can also be employed with nuclear spectra that exhibit slow dynamics, an area where time-domain spectroscopy is not as effective. Ultimately, this approach paves the way for the development of new techniques that combine the benefits of optical and radiowave nuclear physics. It allows for a thorough investigation of nuclear states that have been rapidly excited, an area of study that has been limited by a lack of adequate measurement techniques. It also makes possible the reconstruction of energy spectra with an optimal level of precision in situations where scattering by a coherent light wave is not predominant. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. As such, we anticipate that this framework will prove a valuable tool for the quantum computing community as we work to develop and operate these systems accurately.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the form of a honeycomb lattice. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique filtering effects on the orbits, breaks spatial symmetry, and produces the desired exotic quantum properties. A key characteristic of this system is its large-gap of around 0.36 eV, alongside isolated Dirac cones on the edges which indicate potential applications for room temperature spin-transport. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The major benefits of our approach include its versatility with regards to fracture configuration and layout, as well as its capability to handle essentially non-conforming meshes in regards to blocking fractures. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  Furthermore, by analyzing the temperature dependence of the excited state population, we determined that there is a significant thermally activated shallow donor state about 0.1 electron volts in height.  These results provide insights into the intrinsic and extrinsic properties of this system and may have implications for optimizing the performance of diamond-based quantum technology under high-temperature conditions.  By manipulating this system with external magnetic fields, we also observed the shift of the ODMR resonance and detected the emergence of a new quantum state through a correlation function measurement.  Our study highlights the capabilities and potential of combining optical and nuclear magnetic resonance techniques for exploring the phenomena in this system.  By applying this multi-disciplinary approach, we were able to uncover new features in the system and demonstrate the resilience of diamond-based quantum sensors in extreme environments.  This approach may be extended to investigate other solid-state quantum systems. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. The developed approach offers a high-degree of parallelization, making it an ideal framework for large-scale calculations within the self-consistent field methodology. The implementation, named FENGO, is an open-source code available for download and can be used in conjunction with the FINITE ELEMENT DIRECT METHOD (FIDM) finite-size code for robust convergence analyses. The algorithms and techniques used for developing FENGO could also be applied to other convergence methods based on finite basis set expansions. The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems. This also opens up possibilities for employing natural and artificial systems that exhibit dual stability in a therapeutic or technological context. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, numerical experiments demonstrate the relationship between land-scape regions and optimization trajectories. PMID:#:NOTEořanslationID.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources. Furthermore, we propose that detecting the gravitational wave spectrum from long-lived objects like cosmic strings can serve as a probe of fundamental particle physics parameters, ultimately providing more stringent constraints on the universe's early conditions through various UV extensions of the Standard Model, for example the case of supersymmetry, where the scale of scalar moduli and gravitino masses could be constrained up to 10^10 GeV, or models of only-gravitationally-interacting particles and their reheating temperature, or dark photons with an incredibly low kinetic mixing of 10^-18. Consequently, over the course of the next decade, gravitational wave detectors will significantly improve these models' understanding at the highest possible energy scales. Nonetheless, an incredible number of 10^12 distinct spectral patterns will emerge as a result of the various possible scenarios, making it essential to develop effective analysis methods in the face of such vast possibilities. In our research, we have developed the very first approach to confronting such a multitude of scenarios with the fundamental properties of gravitational wave spectra, specifically the phenomenon of UV decoupling, where we found that we could model the entire background spectrum using only a small set of parameters, specifically those related to the chemical potentials of the various particle species, or in some cases, the fundamental parameters of the underlying theories themselves. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. Additionally, our study shows that in viscoelastic fluids, the'snowman effect' is not only sufficient to explain the observed behavior but also indicates that swimmer design could be optimized for maximum performance in these fluids. This could potentially lead to the development of more efficient microswimmers that can navigate a wide range of fluids with ease. Lastly, our research highlights the significant role that fluid elasticity plays in interacting with ambient turbulence and swimming organism symmetry.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. Full results are presented with rigorous statistical analysis to provide strong evidence supporting our claims. The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. These findings highlight the destructive impact of combining different models on a connected graph, leading to a deviation from the expected result of zero magnetization observed in isolated systems. This research is an exploration of the dynamic interactions within a multi-agent system and raises questions about the effectiveness of extracting physical parameters from simulations of systems of combined models. In such cases, a more in-depth analysis is required than simply multiplying equilibrium parameters by concentration. In the case discussed here, the behavior varies significantly between a fully connected graph and a random graph. In the latter, the effect of increasing the temperature is more complex and depends on the number of Ising agents. These considerations underscore the importance of distinguishing between systems in equilibrium and those out of equilibrium, and highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to tackling complex systems that combine different models. In such multi-agent systems, mean field theory can be an unreliable guide and other methods are required to gain a deeper understanding. In the context of opinion formation, this understanding is crucial for developing more effective policies that take into account the diverse nature of individual agents and their interactions within a society. In the broader context of statistical mechanics, this research represents a step towards investigating systems out of equilibrium and combining different models on complex networks, and for extracting new universality classes from the behavior of such systems. In this way, the study of multi-agent systems is seen as an opportunity to deepen our understanding of the fundamental principles of statistical mechanics, and to broaden the field itself. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, our research highlights the importance of considering the effects of flow on the evaporation of droplets, which could lead to better models for predicting the spread of infectious diseases. Visualizations of our findings are available as supplementary material. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework. As evidence of its practical value, the proposed framework has been successfully utilized in prior research of the author, specifically in fluid dynamics and electromagnetic field mapping projects. The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. Furthermore, we showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to a hypothetical European Parliament transaction graph. Our method has been found to outperform mainframe-based existing systems in both speed and memory usage. A prototype of the proposed algorithm has been implemented using C++ and is available for open public review. Additionally, we have created an open-source prototype of the proposed algorithm and made it available on GitHub. Consequently, we believe that graph algorithms have the potential to be utilized in clearing and netting processes in various other domains. Moreover, we have launched a public discussion on the subject, inviting experts to share their thoughts and collaborate with us in exploring more possibilities. The discussion can be accessed via the GitHub repository. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and clusters across languages. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. All code and data are freely accessible at https://github.com/zhunghuang/mcsm.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Available data through 30% neutron 
multiplicity range will be analyzed utilizing EPOS AUDD and PYTHIA NLO 
solids, with predictions for future low-multiplicity Xe-Xe collisions.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. Under ideal noise conditions, we demonstrate that JWST can determine this line strength with high accuracy and may be capable of identifying regions with high rates of star formation formation, although further analysis is required to fully utilize its potential in this area. Nonetheless, even without additional analysis, we find that observing this line with JWST can provide a accurate, dust-insensitive star formation rate estimate that is in agreement with existing formulas. This new approach to measuring star formation rates is important because it will become a key science goal for future near-infrared galaxy surveys with JWST. Finally, we find that even with the noise levels associated with ground-based near-infrared observations, the equivalent star formation rates can be determined to a reasonable accuracy with existing instruments, assuming adequate signal-to-noise levels, although such results are less robust than those obtained with JWST. Ultimately, this research validates the use of the Prospector framework to determine star formation rates and suggests alternative approaches for interpreting its results. This research is also enabling the development of empirical algorithms to estimate star formation rates in galaxy spectra and providing a basis for related work on the interpretation of stellar spectra. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the complete description for some specific cases with low degrees in a small number of variables.
