In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. We discovered that certain constraints can limit deviation from expected neutrino behavior to below $10^{-3}$, exceeding current limits on a similar problem related to other subatomic particles. However, if we consider only certain other constraints, large unitarity violations can occur and be confirmed or disproven with the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment in a significant margin of error. We propose that findings related to this issue be treated as separate components of a multi-dimensional vector, to be thoroughly analyzed across different neutrino experiments. This insight enables a more precise prediction to be made about the ability of upcoming experiments to provide clear answers to this question. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Brzozowski's derivative operator is already known for its efficiency in solving containment issues with basic regular expressions. With this extended version, we prove that Brzozowski's derivatives still provide a looser, yet stronger guarantee for containing sets defined by enhanced regular expressions. This stronger guarantee enables us to solve inequalities of the form $RE_1 \subseteq RE_2$ when both $RE_1$ and $RE_2$ are regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets, provided that one of the expressions contains a character that does not belong to the other. Additionally, our results demonstrate that determining containment with regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets is computationally complex, specifically NP-complete. Nevertheless, our algorithm remains efficient for practical purposes, given the limited input sizes typically involved. Moreover, our approach can be applied to contain issues with regular expressions over finite character sets, albeit in a less efficient manner, by employing Brzozowski's derivatives in combination with Antimirov's rewriting strategy and the length of shortest distinguishing words for finite sets of characters. We also present an effective implementation of our algorithm, along with accompanying tools that can be found at https://github.com/alexxxl/containment-regex. A theoretical discussion on complex regular expressions containing infinite character sets is also presented, along with an analysis of our approach's computational complexity. Finally, we report on experimental evaluations of our algorithm. Despite the difficulty of determining containment with infinite character sets, our approach remains efficient for practical purposes, given the limited input sizes typically involved. However, further research is needed to address additional features and more complex scenarios. Moreover, possible extensions to address inequality issues with regular expressions over infinite character sets are also discussed. As a result, our approach provides an innovative, efficient, and effective solution to the containment problem with regular expressions, encompassing standard, enhanced, and infinitely vast character sets

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Moreover, this algorithm exhibits better performance and lower training/ inference times than equivalent recurrent models. All the code and data used in this research are available online at https://github.com/strawhensy/AttentionVIO.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. All implementations utilize the free and open-source freefem++ software. No additional tools are used in this research.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail. Moreover, we provide the explicit form of the conformal vector, and establish the 't Hooft anomalies for our algebra, which align with expectations based on the Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$. Our findings also correlate with predictions derived from the anomaly matching principle. Furthermore, we establish that our algebra contains a subalgebra isomorphic to $sl(2)$, whose generators exhibit periodicity. This feature gives rise to an equivariant $N=2$ superVirasoro algebra, whose generators are expressed in terms of our initial generators. Our research is complemented by an invitation to explore connections with twisted modules and twisted parafermion algebras. Our study initiates but does not conclude the examination of the vertex operator algebra structure of the highest weight modules for all integrable representations of $osp(1|2n)$. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Moreover, FedSA exhibits robust performance when confronted with datasets of varying quality. To facilitate further research, the code and datasets associated with this project have been made publicly accessible. As a pioneering effort in Federated Learning where interactions involve both selective data and model exchange, FedSA has the potential to lay the groundwork for future studies in Federated Learning beyond single-task applications. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. Consequently, we suggest that the presence of magnetic cycles be used as an indicator to distinguish between rotational regimes in solar-type stars. Conditions necessary for this approach include sufficient observational datasets and a understanding of how magnetic cycles manifest in radial velocity signals. If these requirements can be met, we propose that magnetic cycles could become a crucial tool for identifying rotational regimes in solar-type stars. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Interestingly, this lower bound is directly applicable to unitary dynamics as well. Finally, we illustrate the concepts and results through examples involving spontaneous emission, unitary dynamics, and the interplay between unitary and non-unitary processes. Our general framework can be applied to multi-level systems and may contribute to a better understanding of quantum state evolution and its relation to asymmetry measures. Our study also raises questions about the universality of bounds expressed in terms of average entanglement or other asymmetry measures.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. By understanding and controlling the terahertz properties at the microscale, we can optimize device performance and reduce heating rates during qubit operations. Upcoming quantum computers requiring robust, coherent operations will benefit significantly from this research. By addressing material flaws causing decoherence, we can harness the full potential of superconducting quantum computing. Ultimately, this will pave the way for scalable, reliable quantum systems capable of delivering genuine quantum advantage.

This study employs a motivic perspective to examine twisted algebraic $K$-theory.
For a variety over a zero-characteristic field and an Azumaya algebra over that
variety, we develop the $\mathcal{A}$-twisted motivic spectral sequence.
By determining the motivic twisted algebraic $K$-theory spectrum as a twisted form
of motivic cohomology, our work expands upon earlier results by Kahn-Levine where the
algebra is derived from a base field.
Our methods utilize a combination of slice filtration and birational geometry to achieve this,
resulting in a representability theorem that expresses twisted $K$-theory space as
an extension of twisted Grassmannian by the twisted integers sheaf.
These results in turn enable proof of cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted
homotopy $K$-theory. Leveraging this, we prove the vanishing of twisted $K$-theory for
smooth projective varieties over fields of characteristic zero, and derive consequences
relating to twisted birational projective varieties and hyperkähler manifolds.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Prioritizing these research goals will help shape future Venus exploration missions and ultimately enable a deeper comprehension of this highly interactive and multifaceted planet system.

Investigating the chemistry occurring on charged droplets offers valuable insights into enhancing industrial chemical production methods, a phenomenon common in nature. To address this, researchers have developed a novel method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. By leveraging ultrashort laser pulses, they have established the capability to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing two types of propanediol isomers, revealing that certain conditions produce a significantly increased yield of methyl ions. Simulation results indicate that this increase results from an optimal molecular alignment on the droplet's surface in one isomer, paving the way for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets. Ultimately, this approach may enable the detection of droplet-based biological systems at a molecular level. A key aspect of this research is the availability of a computer program that simulates reaction nanoscopy data, enabling the interpretation of experimental results. This program can be downloaded from an online repository as part of an open-source license. In addition, a demonstration program has been developed to showcase the functionality of this research, and this program, along with instructions and source code, can be obtained from the same online repository as part of a freely accessible license. This approach offers a groundbreaking new way to study the chemistry of charged droplets, and it may have far-reaching implications for our understanding of this phenomenon. This research has been recognized with an award in the field of optical spectrum analysis. Due to the limitations of the previous measurement method, researchers could only obtain data for droplet sizes larger than one micrometer. However, droplets of this size operate in a multi-dimensional reaction regime that is not under complete theoretical control. To gain more control over droplet sizes and shape, researchers have developed a new method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. This approach utilizes ultrashort laser pulses to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field, providing data for droplet sizes as small as 100 nanometers. Simulation results indicate that this method can detect molecular alignment on the droplet's surface and in the surrounding near-field. This approach has demonstrated the sensitivity required for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. In addition, this method has been made available as an open-source tool, enabling researchers to create valuable datasets and advance the field in cancer research. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This study is set within the context of multivariate Hawkes processes, the most widely used point process model, and its results are relevant to the broader class of nonlinear Hawkes processes. Notably, we have investigated both the homogeneous and inhomogeneous cases, addressing fundamental questions regarding the estimation of process parameters, the convergence of Bayesian estimators, and the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating connectivity graphs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Bayesian methods in addressing significant challenges associated with event-data analysis.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. The code is openly available at: https://github.com/zwang84/CS-CADA. The project page is at: https://zwang84.github.io/CS-CADA/.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. Additionally, potential applications for this component are also being explored for other areas, such as the improvement of laser pulse compression and the reduction of far-field divergence. A numerical model is presented, and experimental demonstration is suggested for this concept. A discussion on possible fabrication methods for the plasma waveplate, including electron beam writing and laser ablation, is also presented. A proposed design along with potential challenges and advantages in various configurations is also discussed. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we explore the relationship between Gelfand and MacPherson's approach and the classical definition of differentiable manifolds through smooth maps from simplicial spheres. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of the pull-back Pontrjagin classes under such maps, including their relationship to transverse pairs and intersections of submanifolds. We also discuss the application of these results to computing the Pontrjagin classes of combinatorial differentiable manifolds, which provides a foundation for further research in computing characteristic classes of differentiable manifolds through their combinatorial representations. We convey the excitement and potential research opportunities that Gelfand and MacPherson's approach has to offer in the field of differentiable topology. We also outline some open questions and related problems for further investigation. Some of these problems have implications in computational topology, a field currently dominated by heuristic algorithms with no theoretical limits. Therefore, answering these questions could provide a foundation for developing algorithms that can handle real-world data inputs in the computation of differentiable manifolds and their invariants. Some of the open questions also relate to the field of string theory and the rich geometric structures that underlie it. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for short-plateau Type II supernovae. However, a striated hydrogen envelope, potentially caused by internal magnetic fields, may have explained the distinctive spectral features in SN~2020jfo. Strikingly, SN~2020jfo displayed a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra similar to another low-luminosity Type II supernova, SN~2008cn. Both supernovae shared similarities in their spectra during the plateau and nebular phases, suggesting a possible connection between their progenitors. Both supernovae exploded at a relatively low velocity and had a mass range of around 12 to 15 solar masses, indicating a specific population of hydrogen-rich Type II supernovae with unusual characteristics. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE design with a single-board, wide-field LE optics was also successfully tested using an X-ray beam. The test revealed that the MuLE board can detect a wide-field X-ray transient with an energy of ~10^-9 erg cm^-2 s^-1 regardless of the source direction. The proposed MuLE optics could potentially reduce the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors by a factor of ~10 to ~20, which may greatly contribute to their space mission weight savings. The MuLE design using four LE mirrors placed at 90-degree rotation angles is set to fly on board the Euclid satellite's XEPS optical system in 2023. The MuLE LE mirrors will be fabricated with a total weight of ~2.3 kg and an area of ~576 cm^2, and will feature a lattice width of 5.8 mm. The MuLE board consisting of four shared image sensors will be able to simultaneously cover a wide field of view of ~10 x 10 degrees with a moderate angular resolution of ~0.18 degrees. We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations. This approach yields an alternative proof of an $L^{\infty}$ estimate for partial uniform ellipticity, a notion introduced by Caffarelli in 2005. Additionally, we demonstrate that a concave fully nonlinear elliptic equation admits continuous solutions when the right-hand side is bounded, extending a result initially validated for strictly concave equations by Cabre and Salsa in 2001. Our methods also provide a new proof of an $L^{\infty}$ estimate for concave fully nonlinear elliptic equations, a result classically known since the work of Serrin in 1979. The main techniques employed are the classical results for concave equations, together with a technique developed by the second-named author to manage level sets. This technique has a complementary flavour to the methods employed by Caffarelli in his studies. The developed strategies open up the possibility for investigating other types of equations involving partial uniform ellipticity.

A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Additionally, when comparing deep learning predictions to ``splash'' plots of actual simulations, notable improvements in accuracy were observed, especially in regions with significant velocity field impact. Ultimately, this study showcases the capability of deep learning to explore intricate features of cosmological simulations and highlights the necessity of velocity field information under certain conditions of varying initial power spectrum conditions. By incorporating velocity information, insights into the halo collapse process can be gained that would otherwise go undetected by models limited to density information alone. By leveraging multiple features, including velocity and density information, a more detailed and nuanced picture of the universe can be gained, allowing for the identification of features that would otherwise remain hidden when analyzing these datasets in isolation. Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Nonetheless, this research provides useful insights into incorporating side information and low-rank constraints within low-rank factorization methods, also applicable to other Music Transcription contexts. The source code is available online for replication purposes.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These models serve as crucial steps towards developing our ultimate goal: a numerical method for solving the nonlinear Euler and Einstein equations through a Lagrangian formulation during quasi-static evolutionary processes within rotating stars. 

Our approach has been applied to construct a wide array of equilibrium configurations, including poloidal-toroidal configurations, differential rotation configurations, stellar models undergoing cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, and binary systems that are sub-merged in a stellar context. These models have been utilized to investigate processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, and our results have demonstrated the capability of our approach to capture the interplay between gravity, rotation, and external electromagnetic forces across diverse configurations. 

Furthermore, our method has been validated through comparisons with existing numerical solutions, as well as analytical approximations, and has been found to maintain overall similarity with established numerical approaches, including the conventional Eulerian method. Nevertheless, our approach has been found to possess distinct advantages, including greater flexibility, better suited for complex processes, and the ability to preserve initial conditions more effectively. 

Ultimately, our research on this novel numerical approach is intended to serve as a key step towards the development of a more advanced numerical method for solving the nonlinear Euler and Einstein equations through a Lagrangian formulation during quasi-static evolutionary processes within rotating stars. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. Further work aims to enhance the network's performance with more candidates and likely detections. We also explore alternative network architectures and a fascinating phenomenon observed during training. This work lays the groundwork for future applications of this deep learning approach in gravitational wave research, including enhancing detector characterization and identifying candidate events. We have made the code publicly accessible to facilitate its utilization by other researchers and contribute to the advancement of machine learning in gravitational wave physics. This code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zbjia/ConvNet-Gravitational-Waves. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Alongside these specific research findings, this work also introduces a framework that can be applied to any study aiming to analyze diversity of a continuous distribution based on group identities, drawing from techniques of conditional mean estimation and treatment effects with a continuous outcome variable. This approach is adaptable to existing research on income diversity of interaction maps by facilitating the examination of diversity based on geographic instead of social attributes. As a result, this study can investigate how diversity within communities varies within a map and provide community annotations for high-density areas. Ultimately, this work is a initial step towards a broader research on promoting diversity of encounters within urban settings, with an expandable framework that can be utilized for an extensive array of measures of diversity. Furthermore, it is observed that when accounting for building attenuation and assuming 5G's maturity, its exposure rates significantly surpass pre-5G exposure. Ultimately, this framework is seen as a useful tool for responsible 5G deployment and communication with concerned communities. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Specifically, we show significant improvements in annotator-agreement levels and overall annotation quality following the BERT-guided process. Moreover, we observe that BERT's evaluations can pinpoint specific annotation errors and contribute to the development of more precise annotation guidelines, leading to better annotation quality with less annotation expertise. As a consequence, a relatively small number of BERT-trained models can cover multiple annotation tasks. Ultimately, we propose an efficient, multi-task annotation framework that accelerates the creation of large-scale, linguistically rich datasets by integrating the following steps: (1) quality control, (2) value correction, and (3) new annotation training, all seamlessly integrated to tackle each annotation task. We hope this work to facilitate the development of advanced neural models and diverse, well-annotated datasets that can fuel progress in nuanced linguistic understanding. As proof-of-concept, we present a dataset called EMO20Q-extended, a expanded version of EMO20Q. Furthermore, we provide a detailed, replicable protocol that includes the code for our approach, thereby making it easy for other researchers to build upon this work and explore the capabilities of this BERT-guided annotation framework. In addition, we introduce a new game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q-extended, consisting of labeled dialog data, to assess a wide range of semantic labels, which is freely accessible for download. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our research involves implementing two reduction methods for the monolithic and partitioned approaches and comparing their efficacy in terms of solution accuracy and computational cost. These findings will provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of RBMs across different FSI methods. Additionally, we'll compare our results with a fixed point strategy for the partitioned approach to further assess the methods' performance. To facilitate replication of these results, the developed software is available for download. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. However, several factors complicate this goal, including the need for ultra-low magnetic noise in the environment surrounding the superconductor and special precautions to prevent atomic spin precession induced by other sources. Nonetheless, this concept opens up the possibility of using atomic interferometry to analyze the Meissner effect in more detail. Furthermore, this approach could also enable the detection of magnetic field expulsion in other superconducting materials that do not easily transition to a permanent Meissner state, such as thin films that require alternative observation methods. Ultimately, this could potentially enable the indirect assessment of these materials' stability and integrity. A theoretical description of a relevant atomic interferometry experiment is outlined in detail, along with the associated system's noise analysis, and this framework is applied to a specific experiment designed to measure the local magnetic field expelled from a superconducting ring in a persistent current state. Finally, this research is placed within the broader context of atomic interferometry applications and its potential to contribute to the development of future high-precision magnetic field measurement systems. This work is part of the author's thesis research.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy for energies beyond MoTe$_2$-EuO's bandgap. Adjusting the chemical potential enables MCE manipulation to induce heating or cooling based on spin orientation across distinct energy valleys. Notably, the Rashba field has contrasting effects, enhancing MCE in the valence zone while diminishing it in the conduction band. This phenomenon of exchange field-induced MCE could lead to the development of magnetic, thermally tunable 2D materials with spin-polarized responses. Furthermore, we propose possible experiments to observe this phenomenon. Additionally, we explore the potential of MCE in MoTe$_2$ layers stacked on other ferromagnetic substrates, such as CoO, CoO/EuO, and GdO, as well as consider implications for magnetic memory devices utilizing 2D materials. Finally, we suggest stacking MoTe$_2$ on non-magnetic insulators with a gap larger than its own to prevent MCE diminishment, and propose alternative designs to amplify exchange field-induced MCE. Overall, this study reveals the capabilities of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides as magnetic, thermally tunable materials with spin-polarized responses, offering implications for memory devices and other applications. Additionally, we identify suitable substrates for exchange field-induced MCE in MoTe$_2$ layers, and propose a non-magnetic multilayer structure to enhance this effect. A potential design for magnetic memory devices is also presented, and we suggest stacking MoTe$_2$ on non-magnetic insulators with a sufficient gap to prevent MCE diminishment, as well as alternative designs to amplify exchange field-induced MCE. A suitable substrate for this effect in MoTe$_2$ layers is also identified, and its capabilities considered. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finds further support through a numerical simulation of light propagation in complex nanojoints. Ultimately, we recommend utilizing a hydrodynamics model that accounts for electron spillover and includes an equivalent reduced gap size to accurately predict light propagation in metallic areas with gaps.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, this treatment is designed to serve as a precursor to a more in-depth examination of the dependent matching operation's properties within the context of the Calculus of Constructions. This research was initially presented at the Dependents '12 workshop in Copenhagen.

This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics. These studies can be applied to various one-dimensional systems, directly relating the electron interactions to the system's topological transport properties.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary. Comparing this to a proposed alternative involving Gaussian processes, we demonstrate that our method results in reduced mean squared error. Furthermore, when weights are known, our method recovers the original components exactly. Through simulation results, we show that our proposed method outperforms established techniques such as noise-free estimation and univariate DP-based methods. We also present a method for wrapping our algorithm within a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework, enabling us to estimate the unobserved components directly. Finally, we apply this to real-world data, including one set of data previously used in a related paper. We observe that our results outperform those paper's findings. We have made our code publicly available.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. As a result, the study provides a detailed explanation for the threshold resummation technique used in ref. [22]. The proposed approach also offers a framework for directly obtaining threshold terms in flat-space scattering amplitudes via AdS amplitude calculations. As a demonstration, the model is employed to derive the two-loop correction to the BPS trajectory in N=4 SYM theory, confirming the previously obtained results. The study concludes with an investigation of the AdS/CW duality at two loops, demonstrating that the predicted entanglement entropy values accurately match the results derived from the holographic projection of AdS amplitudes. The framework has the potential to further explore the relationship between AdS amplitudes and entanglement entropy in general cases. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  In addition, DynaSOAr has been successfully applied to real-world applications, including an order-1 Hessian matrix evaluation for a linear regression system with 100k features, where it computed 1.6 gigabytes of data in 0.27 seconds on a single GPU.  The framework's simplicity is further highlighted by its ease of adoption for average developers, as evidenced by our developer experience survey, where all participants were able to easily integrate DynaSOAr into their code within 30 minutes.  Finally, our research is continuing to evolve with ongoing optimizations, new features, as well as explorations into parallelizing multi-method applications across distinct objects in a given class. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. These predictions provide valuable insights for interpreting experimental outcomes involving Mn impurities on the Nb(110) surface.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Our code and models are available for download at https://github.com/yinumo/FourierMask.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. Additionally, we found that clouds with cores greater than about 30 optical scales in diameter are generally optically thick and may be treated as infinitely thick. These findings may lead to advances in cloud tomographic reconstruction and facilitate further development of this technique for analyzing complex clouds from space. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron void. Additionally, our experiment features an auxiliary thin layer with low density, situated behind the main target layer. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated into a mono-energetic beam by the electrostatic field generated in the main target under interaction with a negatively frequency-modulated, highly intense laser pulse, achieving protons with maximum energies of around 100 MeV when subjected to specific optimal conditions involving a 10-fs, intensively Gaussian pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak intensity. Our experimental findings demonstrate the effectiveness of frequency modulation in achieving efficient ion acceleration from thin, sub-wavelength targets with multiple-layer density distributions.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. This finding highlights the diversity of planetary formations during the early stages of planetary system development. Systems similar to TOI-712 may be discovered through follow-up missions such as $LUVOIR$, a proposed NASA mission that can study planetary systems in search of life on planets within their hosts' habitable zones. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively. Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, it was determined that gas density in the CMZ is significantly influenced by anisotropic spatial patterns at a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. These patterns decrease in anisotropic influence as the scale diminishes to about 10 parsecs. Our research offers a quantitative assessment of the anisotropic structure in gas within the CMZ and provides a method for comparing similar regions in various areas of the galaxy. Additionally, this method may be applied to study the anisotropic distribution of objects such as molecular clouds, young stars, and supernova remnants in the CMZ. By using this approach in the future, we aim to monitor any changes in the anisotropic patterns of these entities over time. By doing so, we hope to gain insights into their lifetimes and movements. Up-to-date satellite imagery of the galaxy, specifically the Spitzer and WISE maps, was utilized to investigate potential causes of the anisotropic patterns. By analyzing these images, we propose a theory that the density structure of gas in the CMZ is shaped by a pair of massive lobes located near the galaxy's center, associated with a supermassive black hole located at the heart of the Milky Way. These lobes appear as areas of reduced infrared emission and are referred to as the Galactic Center Lobes (GCLs). Clouds within the CMZ tend to avoid moving directly towards or away from the galaxy's center due to the influence of the GCLs, thereby maintaining an anisotropic distribution. By modeling the GCLs as a non-interacting potential and considering the stars and gas within the CMZ to be distinguishable, we calculated the anisotropic influence of the GCLs on nearby molecular clouds using their cross-correlation function. Our findings indicate that the GCLs' influence is visible up to a distance of approximately 60 parsecs and suggest that the CMZ's anisotropic structure at this scale can be attributed to the presence of the GCLs.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we discovered that infrared dark clouds exhibit a higher ratio of protostellar cores among their core populations when compared to visual dark clouds.  This distinction may be a key factor in the differences in core populations seen between these two types of molecular clouds.  By analyzing core pairs within the Dragon infrared dark cloud, we found evidence supporting the concept of core-companion interactions as a source of outflow momentum enhancement.  However, more extensive observational and theoretical studies are required to fully understand these processes.  In the case of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, we found that core-companion interactions may also contribute to the formation of massive protostars, offering an additional pathway to the formation of massive stars.  Finally, our analysis revealed a prominent radio source associated with the water outflow from the core CGPKN-N1 within the Dragon infrared dark cloud, a finding that highlights the need for follow-up observations in the radio and far-infrared across the entire cloud complex. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The stick-slip regime is also influenced by the distribution of surface area between the apexes of asperities and the bases surrounding Plateau borders. The implications of our findings are relevant to improving the rigidity of foam structures and understanding friction patterns in other complex liquids over rough surfaces. Additionally, stress fluctuations in stick-slip scenarios can lead to significant vibrations across the system. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed methods also demonstrate superiority over scheduling the look-ahead in the decoder layer schedule strategy. The code has been made available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhunghuizhi/look-ahead-attention.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our predictions for various cosmic parameters for the immediate and distant future are in line with several past studies. Ultimately, our model predicts a future dominated by dust, along with a eventual return to a state of cosmological stability. A thorough comparison with several popular dark energy models has validated our model's viability. Nevertheless, further experimentation through the development of more refined models is still needed to confirm our findings. Our model's code is available upon request. Our analysis contributes to a better comprehension of unified dark fluid models and encourages the development of additional research in this area. Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is further illustrated through the application of these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to two specific problems. This includes the estimation of hidden stable velocities from observable positions in spatial domains, and the recognition of latent traits from observable characteristics in social networks. This innovative work expands the potential applications of Gaussian processes while also providing a framework that is easily extensible to various other graph-based settings.
